review_text: Torres del Paine National Park is found between the Andes Mountain range and the Patagonian Steppe in the Chilean side of Patagonia. It covers an area of just over 1800 sq km (700 sq mi). The National Park holds within its boundaries a number of glaciers, lakes, rivers and valleys, as well as the famed centerpiece, Cordillera del Paine, where we found the two most recognized rock formations known as Las Torres (the three towering rock formations that give the park its name) and Cuernos del Paine (the Paine Horns). The park is located about 112 km (70 mi) north of the town of Puerto Natales and approximately 312 km (194 mi) north of the city of Punta Arenas. Commercial flights in Chile only fly into the city of Punta Arenas, where you must then take a bus or transfer to the town of Puerto Natales, before continuing to Torres del Paine. Transfers from Punta Arenas to Puerto Natales takes anywhere between 2 1/2 to 3 hours, and then it is another 1 1/2 to 2 hours to get to Torres del Paine National Park. For the longest time, visiting Torres del Paine National Park was reserved for backpackers and hikers willing to 'rough-it'. Accommodations across the National Park were very basic and in order to really see the best sites of the Park you had to spend several nights in tents and refuges around the main trails and circuits. However, as of the last 8 years, this has really changed. New hotels, lodges and very comfortable camping sites have been built all around the Park, allowing almost anyone the chance to see one of the most beautiful National Parks in the World. I read that over 4 million people from all over the world voted on a recognized travel website and named Torres del Paine as the 8th Wonder of the World! Which I would easily vote the same! Today you can visit Torres del Paine in 2 ways: The first is by staying in hotels around around the Park and venturing out on daily excursions to the most famous visitor sites, and the second is by doing the entire W or the O Trekking Circuits around the Paine massif. The entire Park contained clearly marked paths and many refuges and camping sites which provided basic services and shelter for backpackers. These circuits took us anywhere between 6 to 12 days to complete, depending on the pace and the activities you wish to do along the way. How you choose to see Torres del Paine National Park really depends on your budget, your physical condition and on how you wish to experience the Park. Activities offered around the Park range from walks and hikes, to horseback riding, to kayaking, to fly fishing, to navigations across lakes and more. You can see and do it all if you give yourself enough time and plan properly like we did! The views in the park are absolutely breathtaking and I would recommend this to anyone who really appreciates nature in its purest form. Visiting Torres del Paine is recommended during the months of October thru April. During these months the weather is nicer, and daylight hours are long, due to the extreme southern latitude. During the Patagonian Winter (May – August) many trails close and the weather can get too cold for trekking.

review_text: One of the oldest Salsa Places in Santiago. Some people think that Santiago is off the Salsa world. Not true at all, if you like Salsa and Latin Dances there are several places where you can practice, learn, and enjoy. Maestra Vida with its old. fashioned Havana alike look, is an interesting place to visit. Open mostly from wednesdays to sundays, you can enjoy local and foreign salsa and latin bands, or the classic saturdays and sundays dance nights. Lots of foreigners, interesting people. In one of the busiest corners in Barrio Bellavista. Classic salsa is the sound of the night . Don't expect pop-salsa, bachata or merengue, as they rarely play it.

review_text: Our 4 full day Antarctica cruise with AntarcticaXXI was completely CANCELLED due to weather. Be very careful with this company and review your contract of carriage with AntarcticaXXI. Upon our arrival in Puntas Arenas, our entire cruise to Antarctica was CANCELLED due to weather. AntarcticaXXI will keep 40% of your entire ticket price to defray their company costs. For instance, a double cabin that cost $30,000 means AntarcticaXXI will keep $12,000 in their pocket for the CANCELLED trip. They will claim you agreed to their Contingency Plan Program for delayed flights to Antarctica. What is not clear is that if AntarcticaXXI CANCELS your trip they will keep 40% of your paid ticket. Francesco Contini, EVP Sales & Marketing, will Fed Ex you an apology letter telling you he is sorry your trip did not operate. What is missing in the apology letter is my check for $12,000 completing my full refund for services not rendered. (Trip cost $30,000) Personally, this is just bad business. Based on AntarcticaXXI's inability to do the right thing by refunding our full ticket prices I can not in good conscience recommend anybody to do business with this company. Francesco... is $12,000 worth a 1 star rating on TripAdvisor to you? Apparently, the answer is YES!!! Between January 28 and January 31, 2015 heavy fog did not permit the operation of any flights to King George Island, the gateway for ANTARCTICA XXI's expeditions. As a result, the departure scheduled to fly to Antarctica on January 28, and arranged for a photographic group, lost the opportunity for a visit to Antarctica. Although never before in the company’s 12-year history have weather conditions delayed a flight to the point of preventing participants from reaching Antarctica, the promotional brochure for the expedition outlined a detailed plan in case of delays. This plan was featured in a dedicated and clearly visible section titled “Contingency Plan” (i.e. not in the “fine print”). It followed the “Important Information” section that strongly recommended the purchase of travel insurance. It stated that in case unfavourable weather would delay the operation of the Antarctic flight, participants would wait in Punta Arenas for an opportunity to fly. The services that would be provided were outlined. It continued by stating that “If by the end of Day 7 (24:00 hours local time) ANTARCTICA XXI will not be able to transport passengers to Antarctica, ANTARCTICA XXI will refund to each passenger 60% of the total rate (excluding discounts, if any) paid for the voyage.” The conditions of the Contingency Plan reflected the nature of the expedition and the complexity of the operation. The 64 participants in this unlucky departure received accommodation and airport transfers in Santiago, round-trip flights from Santiago to Punta Arenas, transportation, meals, and accommodation in Punta Arenas. They received a private excursion on a chartered boat on the Strait of Magellan, as well as other organized excursions in Punta Arenas and surroundings. During the entire time seven acclaimed photography instructors who flew to Punta Arenas from the USA, Canada, Australia, and Great Britain accompanied participants. Emergency mobile phones were provided to participants while in Punta Arenas. A team of 3 front-line staff members from ANTARCTICA XXI escorted and coordinated the group, booking meeting rooms and holding briefings, while a back-office team supported them 24/7. In the flight operations department, meteorologists and veteran Antarctic pilots worked tirelessly, monitoring the weather and preparing flight plans, only to be repeatedly frustrated by persistent fog at King George Island. In Antarctica, a logistics team was on standby at King George islands ready to receive the flight, while a fully provisioned ship with 38 officers, crew, chefs, hotel staff, and 12 polar guides waited for the group to arrive. That is the reason the Contingency Plan is structured as it is. While the conditions of the Contingency Plan were clearly presented prior to reservation, ANTARCTICA XXI has gone beyond. Firstly, with no improvement in the weather conditions in sight, on January 31 ANTARCTICA XXI arranged a charter flight from Punta Arenas to Santiago, as well as airport transfers and accommodation in Santiago. This charter flight was not part of the original itinerary nor of the Contingency Plan. It was organized by ANTARCTICA XXI to provide our valued clients the opportunity to return home as soon as possible, without waiting for the scheduled commercial flights on February 4, thereby avoiding further delay and frustration. Secondly, in conjunction with the group organizers we are developing a special offer designed to offer participants in this unlucky departure the chance to join a future expedition at a significant discount. Everyone at ANTARCTICA XXI deeply regrets that the weather conditions did not allow the operation of the Antarctic flight. We feel for the disappointment experienced by participants, as it is our disappointment also. We recognize that the circumstances our company faced were challenging. But we did everything we could and we cannot see how ANTARCTICA XXI can be blamed in any way for what happened. Francesco Contini Executive Vice President, Sales & Marketing

review_text: Although the village is a replica of Parinacota village in the Altiplano, it does give a faithful impression of the lovely architecture - not everyone will be able to travel above 4,000M to visit the real thing... We visited to find handmade items made truly in the region and we were not disappointed. There were two shops we liked in particular, one was a shop with ceramics, including handmade terracotta replica's of the Missionary Altiplano church towers, they are actually really nicely made, they make very nice little souvenirs. We met the man who makes them who lives in the little house next to the shop, they are made on the premises. The other shop we really liked was the outlet of the Asociacion Indigena Red de Artesanal Productoras PUSKA, an organisation set up by women from the Altiplano villages in Chile to preserve and promote their indigenous weaving and wool-dying skills. Most items are in Alpaca wool and just really gorgeous, soft and stylish. We bought a beautiful poncho in pure white Alpaca, a scarf in dog tooth pattern (looks very English funnily enough..) and gloves. Prices utterly reasonable. If you want to support proper hand-made stuff that is local and of high quality, go there. Whilst we were there, a baptism had taken place in the Chapel on the side, and we were able to see inside, very lovely.

review_text: Nacho was our guide. This review is nothing against him. He did a great job and was friendly and informative. The rating is for the misleading description of the tour written by the tour company. This was supposed to be a “small” group tour and it stated that the max capacity was 15 people. That’s why we chose this over the many other tour companies that are out there. We were 23 people crammed into the bus like sardines. Every single seat was occupied. Also, in the description it states that it was a 40 minute drive to the wineries. What they don’t tell you is that if you are one of the unfortunate ones to be picked in the first few pickups, you’re looking at another good hour on the bus. Same with the return trip. Another hour to get you back to your hotel once you get into town (which would not happen if it was truly a “small group”.) It would have at least been more fair to us to drop us off first since we were picked up in the first couple trips. Very unfair to keep us on the bus 2 extra hours in total round trip. Lastly, the most concerning thing for us was the bus driver. It was extremely jerky on the way there which was annoying but on the way to one of the wineries in the middle, the driver hit a speed bump so hard and fast that the people in the back injured their heads on the low roof and my fiancé and I had neck pain from the severe jolt. In summary, the wineries were nice and the wine was fine. Nacho was fine. The last winery was a disappointment as the large group of 23 of was combined with another large group so we were touring and tasting with approximately 50 people. We do not recommend this tour at all. We regret not booking with Pablo (whom we met after we paid), and his company Tours by Locals. We feel disappointed with the dishonesty and safety provided by this company. Review of: Maipo Valley Wine Tour with 4 vineyards from Santiago.

review_text: San Cristobal is definitely a must see for all visitors to Santiago. You can either walk up the hill (via several roads / paths) or take the tram / cable car. The summit has a beautiful statue of the Virgin Mary, which is a landmark of the city, with a great view of Santiago. In summer the view tends to be pretty clear, but the earlier you go the better as the valley is sometimes dusty / smoggy (in winter months) which makes the view less crisp / clear. You'll find several restaurants / snack bars at the top, with good views, and lots of picnic areas. In summer months there is a large public pool as well. The park connects into Parque Metropolitan de Santiago, which includes a series of trails / roads that extends across the cerros all the way to Vitacura (Americo Vespucio Norte). I run these trails with my dogs regularly and they are well-used by locals and very safe for exploring. This is my favourite park in the city of Santiago, hands down, as it is very accessible and extensive.

review_text: After reviewing the sample itinerary and reviews, we booked this tour to see as many things as possible while being able to get back to Santiago for dinner. We didn't get any communication with the operator until the night before the tour, and found the experience disorganized and poorly executed. While some things can certainly be attributed to poor behavior by other tour guests, I cannot recommend anyone book this tour if they are interested in meaningful sightseeing. Some examples of what happened below: -We were told to be ready and outside our hotel at 8:25am. After waiting for 15 minutes, I had to reach out to the operator for an update. Our pickup ended up being 30 minutes late. We made two more pick-up stops before embarking and neither guests were ready so this may be attributed to other guests. -The guide announced we'd make a short 10 minute stop on the way to Vina del Mar to use the restroom and get drinks. This stop ended up taking 25 minutes, and was immediately followed up with an unannounced stop at an off-route fuel station for the bus. This further delayed us. -After very brief stops at the Flower Clock and Moai in Vina del Mar (which, oddly, were positioned as "surprises" by the guide despite being included on the sample itinerary), we were dropped at Caleta Portales where the guide promptly lost half our group and didn't explain why we stopped. The wet market smells were overwhelming and the guide had a hard time corralling guests. -We were driven through Valparaiso with almost no opportunity for a walking tour or photos. We only stopped for a brief walk to a meeting point where we were dismissed for lunch with a strict time to return. -Multiple parties didn't return after lunch. We were further delayed for 20+ minutes waiting for the guide to find all guests. We were then rushed to the funicular and informed our tour would be abbreviated to accommodate the winery reservation. -The tour only included one of the three advertised funiculars (acensor). We don't know how much else from the sample itinerary was missed because the guide was not announcing where we were, or what we were seeing. -Our final stop was Bodegas RE for a wine tasting. We booked our tour specifically because Casablanca Valley is known for white wines. The Bodegas RE tasting included three wines, one rose and two reds. There was no tour of the facility but we were rushed to finish and return to Santiago. The guide made an announcement that we took too long during the tour and not all guests would be dropped at their hotels. -On a final note, the driver Brian seemed to have a better grasp on English than the guide Marcel. The guide constantly turned to the driver or other guests for assistance translating. This language barrier likely contributed to the degraded tour experience. Overall, I was unhappy with my purchase of this tour. That being said, I'm sure other travelers with more mindful groups and better tour guides would have a better experience. I offer you our sincere apologies and I guarantee that we take care your advises because our target is keep doing one of the best tours to Valparaiso that you can find in Chile. Best regards.

review_text: We were pretty apprehensive about sand boarding as we'd never been skiing or snowboarding before so we weren't sure we'd be able to do it. It was so much fun and definitely not as difficult as we thought it would be. The instructor stays with you and gives you as much or as little attention as you want. One thing I would say is that death valley is excruciatingly hot and you have to walk up a good sized dune to board down. Bring as much water as possible with you and if you're in any way unfit, you might struggle slightly with the climb. We would have loved to have done the night boarding but it was unavailable as an option while we were there unfortunately. If this option is open, I'd go with this, might be less hot. All-in-all a great experience.

review_text: I did the W trek with Cascada tours. I LOVED the Ecocamp! The domed tent with nice bed/mattress/blankets were beyond comfortable and the trip was well organized. Food was awesome! The horns and towers were amazingly beautiful, not to mention the endless number of green glacier lakes and waterfalls, The trails were nicely marked and there was no way one could get lost, even without being in a tour group. Every 8-10 miles there was a Refugio/camp site. It was great hiking hut to hut, meals included (if you choose to buy it with your night's stay). Some refugios even had Happy Hour!!! I would come back here in an heart beat... next time probably not joining a tour group as I like to hike at my own pace instead of with 10 other people. I loved the fact that there were no cell towers/airplanes flying overhead. The only thing that had taken me by surprise was the WIND. Some days I had to hang on to my hat and looked down on the ground the whole time because the wind was so fierce. One morning after getting up from my cabin I saw a tent that had gotten blown away, all the way up the hill... no idea where the tent owners had spent the night! It was worth every penny to stay in the refugios vs. camping outside in the howling wind!

review_text: This was the most outstanding whitewater rafting experience I have ever had! The team (Sebastian, Christian and Colyn) was very friendly, very professional and well organized, We spent about one and one half hours rafting the Petrohue river (grade 3 and 4 rapids). Sebastian guided us through the rapids with great aplomb. Christian accompanied us in a kayak as a extra safety measure, in case anybody fell out of the rubber raft. Colyn took some great photographs of our experience, which were sold to us at a reasonable price and accessible through Dropbox. We even had the chance for a short swim in the river, which was warmer than I expected. The scenery was absolutely outstanding, including the Volcàn Osorno and three other volcanoes. Afterwards, we all shared some sandwiches, which we washed down with some cool local beers. Including timely transfers by minibus to and from our hotel in Puerto Varas, the whole experience took a full afternoon. review_text: Having only two days in mid-July to spend in Santiago I went on Trip Advisor to find something to do. I enjoy cycling so I decided to do this tour. It was also a sigh of relief not to be doing the usual bus tour of a big city. The only thing on the downside was the weather. It was cold and raining but we were well prepared so this didn't really matter much. Andres was lovely and his enthusiasm was very apparent. Also, his wife's home cooking was amazing! The soup was especially delightful. The tour definately takes you off the beaten track but also includes the main sites. It really gives you an insight to what it's like to live in Santiago. I would recommend this 5 hour day trip to anyone who is able-bodied. You don't need to be really fit as the city is flat. I also think it would be a good day out for families. (If you are into architeture it would be extra special!) If you are there in winter remember your warm clothes and especially gloves. We were well prepared for the rain as we checked the weather forecast the day before. (Unlucky to get rain in a city where it only rains 15 days a year!) I hope this helps people make up their minds. I would highly recommend this to everyone.

review_text: Cementerio General, where the murdered ex-president Salvador Allende (and many other ex-presidents and notables) is buried, is a huge experience. One of the biggest attractions in Santiago de Chile, actually. It's a whole city - a so-called necropolis - with named streets lined with hundreds of beautifully decorated buildings designed as small palaces, churches, Greek temples, etc. Each of these mausoleums must have been staggeringly expensive, even though they can accommodate entire families, so immortality comes at a price. A very high price. Salvador Allende's sculptural family grave is uniquely timeless in its design. A dignified blend of public memorial and private family grave. In my opinion, Santiago's Cementerio General is even more impressive than the (perhaps) more famous La Recoleta in Buenos Aires, where Evita Peron is laid to rest. Chile's richest families have either been wealthier than their Argentine contemporaries - or more obsessed with the coveted immortality.

review_text: We sent an e-mail and promptly got a response and had a nice chat with Leo, who speaks perfect English. Quintay is where most Chileans learn to dive--close to both Santiago and Valparaiso. The water is cold due to the Humboldt current despite it being the Pacific Ocean. We paid Chilean peso 3,000 per person for one dive to the wrecks (boats associated with the nearby whaling operations that once took place in Quintay and which were apparently sunk in the 1960s) with all equipment included. You can pay by credit card. We booked an uber from Valparaiso and it cost Chilean peso 22,000. Leo helped us book a collective back. You can catch one at the bus station in Valpo starting at 8 AM for 2 or 3,000 per person to the main square in town and then walk to the dive shop. Leo gave us a good dive briefing and we were accompanied by two dive masers. My spouse is on crutches and his staff helped her into the boat and took a lot of care. The equipment is good. They give you a 7 MM and a 5 MM shorty over it as well as gloves and a hood. They also loan you a dive computer. Water temp. was 13C in summer. Colder in winter. They had algae bloom which limited viz a bit. This fades away once the weather cools. They have warm showers, a toilet and they sell coffee, juices and ice cream. Leo also gave us tips on where to eat after our dive. The team here are super friendly and professional.

review_text: What a lovely day we had tasting wine with this wine tour company! I worked with Al prior to our trip to arrange a day of visiting boutique wineries, so our day way planned out. Sebastian was a friendly guide and our driver was excellent. Due to a highway accident, we had to change our schedule and visit one different winery to replace another. Unfortunately, it was a large, run of the mill winery that was really crowded (so crowded they didn't have room for us at a tasting table) and wasn't really what we wanted or picked out for our private tour. We really wanted to focus on small boutique wineries. I would say it wasn't a comparable swap, and the only reason I mention it is b/c I paid quite a bit extra for the previously scheduled winery, and we weren't provided with any compensation back or anything extra to compensate for the modification. I understand it was an unexpected change, and I didn't care about that, and we were totally willing and flexible due to the terrible highway accident. It isn't a huge deal, but I was hoping that it would have been addressed and that is the only reason this wasn't a 5 star rating. Everything else was great. We did hit the other 2 wineries we picked out prior (out of the 3) and they were fantastic experiences and exactly what we wanted. We also gave Sebastian feedback after our visit to the larger winery and told him to not take guests there anymore. He was appreciative of the instant feedback and said he would make note. I highly recommend you book with Al! Make sure you visit the smaller wineries where appointments are needed.

If you want something original, I would advise to go outside the market to the artisanal tables scattered around the outside courtyard. Here you will find hadmade jewelry, pottery, baskets, paintings, etc. La Recova has food upstairs as well as a paid bathroom. To save some dollars, skip eating at La Recova and instead eat at the supermarket right to the market. You can eat for $3 to $4US which will include your selection of meat, potatoes and a small drink.

review_text: They were supposed to pick us up at our hotel at 6am. They weren't replying to my messages and 6am came and went while my husband and I were trying to get ahold of them and waiting for them. So, we were stuck in the town with no way to get back to our hotel. The only way we got back to our hotel finally was because one of the guides was sweet and took us back in his own personal car. Do not book with this company. Choose anyone else. I had a very poor experience with this whole excursion. Their communication is very poor, and they don't care what happens to their guests. review_text: We chose the 4 hour city tour as it offered hotel pickup and hit the high points. Pros: They picked us up early so that the rendezvous/pay/ switch buses routine got everyone on their specific tour on time. The tour was good and the guide enlightened us on the history and politics of Chile. The guide (Donato) spoke English and the two other languages required. We were given plenty of time off the bus. Cons: The amount of walking required-- 90 minutes of walking through the Historic Centre to see the plaza, the cathedral and the beautiful old buildings, move on to the park and more historic edifices. It was not mentioned in the brochure that we would be on our feet that long at one stop. The guide was required to give the talk in 3 languages--which is good- but then the tour was slowed while each group learned the history of the building/statue/cathedral. There was a lot of standing around as the guide didn't want us out of his sight; the children and elderly got a little bored/tired. Traffic required we walk to another pickup point because the tour bus couldn't get through. The "unmissable Cerro Santa Lucia" amounted to it being pointed out when we passed it. The restroom break stop was at a nice art gallery/ plaza with interior courtyard seating. The stop at the Parque Bicentenario was actually a photo stop and not an opportunity to walk around the park. As advertised in the brochure, we paid $20,000CLP per person at the rendezvous point. Reservations were made by our hotel. Many Thanks for your comments. We will be more specific in our next brochure about the walking distance at the Historic Center. Regarding to the Cerro Santa Lucia, unfortunately we were not able to stop cause there was a event, so the authorities closed the entrance to the Cerro. Thanks again for your comments, TurisTour Team,

review_text: The architect Fenado Antequera, aware of the importance of cultural patrimony, was building a hotel when he discovered a cemetery filled with mummies form the chinchorro Culture. In total there were 48 bodies of women, children and men. Due to the extremely delicate condition of these thousand year old bodies, in 2006 the University of Tarapaca bought the property in order to build an on-site museum. This way, you can see the bodies of fishermen of the Chinchorro Culture which date between 4 and 5 thousand years of age according to carbon dating. The Chinchorro lived in the coast from Ilo in Peru to the city on Antofagasta, concentrating mainly on the coasts of Arica to Camarones, where out of the bodies have been found. They were Ainsley gatherers and hunters. They believe there are many more under the roads and surrounding houses. It was emotional to be standing on top of these skeletons and mummies. People come from all over the world just to stop here. Wow....

review_text: We visited this place on our own as we couldn't go to Salar de Tara or Piedras Rojas since the roads were closed due to snow. We walked from our cabin to the Pukara and the road is flat, so it's an easy walk. There are three different paths you can choose from: the view point (quite short); the long one (with the cross on top) and the one taking you to the cave. We did the two first in about 3 hours and 1/2 (counting from the moment we left home). You have beautiful views along the way and it is only 3.000 CLP per person. Make sure you take water, some snacks, sun screen, hat and sunglasses, as there are no shops in the area, but just nearby. The place opens at 8:00 am and closes around 5:00 pm. I recommend this place.

review_text: We booked a City Tour in Santiago with the amazing tour guide Boris. Little did we realize that we would be visiting during the time of protests, uprisings and more - as workers rightfully demanded higher wages to combat income inequality. First off, we always felt safe with Boris. But without prejudice or political leanings, Boris educated us about what was happening and why in Santiago and gave us insights into the complicated structure that makes up Chile both today and historically. The buildings, the parks, the views were all terrific, but even better were Boris' clear and concise analysis. These are tours that don't just show you the sights, but make you understand what's happening and why. review_text: A very beautiful trail through the villages, forests and coast. Started it at 08:00 when the sun came up, went north through the village (cows, ships and horses along the way) and to the coastal trail. The winds made a little sand storms on the coast that made beautiful shapes. The sights were amazing - all green and natural. The trail should take 10-12 hours (both ways). Did it in 6.5 with walking fast and hitchhiking in the village. The trail does'nt have enought signs for not going lost. If there is a question on which direction to go - south on the coast. Take enough cloths to protect you from the rain - it was raining on my way back, lucky i brought coat, pants and bag covers. I liked it that i was alone on the trail - just me, nature and the mp3.

review_text: It is a very long drive (from anywhere) to get to Torres del Paine National Park and if you are coming from Argentina, you must pass through both Argentinian and Chilean customs to do so, which took us an hour and a half. Then there is the cost of 21,000 Chilean pesos per person to enter the park (Whew! But that is only about US$34.00/person). So why would anyone go to such trouble - because the dang place is so absolutely, incredibly, beautiful! As Iguazu Falls is Niagara on steriods, Torres del Paine is Yellowstone on steriods! We believe that if you visit this park, the sight of Main & East Horns will forever remain bright in your memory! And that image will be but one of many! While Mount Fitz Roy is awesome, the number of awesome sights at Torres del Paine is nearly countless; so even El Chalten cannot, in our opinion, compete with Torres del Paine. This is, without doubt, a World Class "By-Itself," MUST SEE!

review_text: Arrived by ship and were whisked off by Boris for a fabulous day of sightseeing, wandering, delicious lunch, wine tasting and delivery to the airport. Our family of 6, plus luggage, were picked up at the cruise dock and taken on a combination van tour and walking tour of Valparaiso. Boris was the perfect tour guide as he knows the area well--he also teaches local cuisine cooking classes in town. We wandered into local shops where he knows the owners, and we went at our own pace. Vina Del Mar was mostly by van, although we stopped off to have our photo with the Easter Island Moai. A nice drive out to the Casablanca Valley had us arriving at the delightful restaurant in time for lunch. Having been introduced to the owner and his son we sipped our Pisco Sours and had a delicious, fresh from the garden, meal. Then onward to the wine tasting at Indomita winery. By the time we were dropped at the airport we were old friends (or new) with hopes for future visits together. For less than half the price we would have paid through the cruise line we had a made-to-order personalized trip. Boris is the best! Book him at Michael the Pirate miguelarno@gmail.com.

The walk to the top takes about 20-30 minutes, depending on the pace, whether you choose to take the stairs or road paths that are gentler and how long you stop at the various places and courtyards to rest and view the surroundings. The very top offers a 360 degrees panoramic view of the city. There is only a small space for visitors to take pictures and with the many coming up to the top, one can't stay on for very long. And besides, there are no seats to rest. Be sure to explore the various courtyards and learn about the history and significance of cerro Santa Lucia. At the end of the walk, treat yourself to a shopping trip to the shops just across the cerro Santa Lucia

review_text: This museum is huge, and has a ton of fun, and very educational, things for kids to do. It has 2 huge levels that include interactive displays with light, sound, optical illusions, electronics, body movement, bubbles, art, gravity, and more. It has a playground outside, and a fun area with multi-colored ribbons for kids to run through. We have taken our daughter twice, (because we live in Santiago), once when she was 18 months, and again when she was 2.5 years, and she has loved it each time. The best thing about it is that is has such a range of things to do that families with several children will be able to keep everyone happy. Kids in high school have fun there, with the more advanced displays, and there is plenty for younger children as well. There is a aquarium there as well, but we've never had time or energy to go after several hours at the MIM, and we've been told by friends who have gone that it is not worth a visit. There is a cafe which has snacks, and you can connect to the museum on the metro, as there is a shuttle from the metro to the museum.

review_text: DO NOT FALL FOR THIS SCAM! I GOT SCAMMED BY THEM! They withhold information, deceive you about the tour, and then, under threats, force you to pay for a service they didn’t deliver, even increasing the originally agreed-upon amount. Their equipment is dirty and unhygienic, and they demonstrate a complete lack of manners, along with criminal acts of moral abuse and coercion against their clients. The experience I had with this agency and with Richard was by far the WORST of my life. I’ve done adventure tourism worldwide and trusted many companies, but nothing—NOTHING—comes close to the utter disrespect, abuse, and rudeness I experienced with these people. I was insulted, verbally abused, and even threatened by him. Let me explain every detail so no one else has to go through what I went through. From the very beginning, I was deceived with incomplete and misleading information about the volcano hike. They told me I only needed to bring my backpack with water, juice, and chocolate. That’s it. I arrived thinking everything was ready, but I was handed a pre-packed backpack stuffed with absurdly heavy equipment, dirty boots, non-adjustable hiking poles, even a sled, and an ice axe that were never used—plus jackets that looked like rags. On top of that, the "guides" just rush ahead, leaving you to fend for yourself. There’s zero care, and we’re talking about a dangerous environment. That’s when things got even worse. After barely walking 50 meters—without even starting the actual hike or reaching the park’s base—I was forced to pay the full amount. There was NOTHING in the documents I signed about fees for quitting, nor was I informed about it when I decided not to proceed (and I only stopped because of the excessive weight of the backpack). To make matters worse, the terms and conditions were only in English—as if, in CHILE, I wouldn’t have the right to a Spanish version! But the worst part was yet to come. Richard, the person in charge, had the audacity to verbally attack me with the worst insults imaginable. Yes, he OFFENDED me, THREATENED me, and CALLED ME NAMES—some of the worst you can think of. He said he’d call the police if I didn’t pay, accused me of being a scammer (when he was the scammer!), and fabricated a list of expenses he supposedly incurred (knowing full well it was a lie). He then, unethically, cursed and insulted me in various ways. To make matters even more DESPICABLE, he said he would deduct the payment from a female employee’s salary if I didn’t pay what he wanted. This man is the worst example of a human being I’ve ever met, and this agency is a total FRAUD. They have zero respect for their clients, treating tourists as if they’re only there to be exploited. I felt robbed and extorted. I’ll never set foot in this place again because of this Chilean man. This isn’t tourism—it’s ABUSE. To make matters worse, the terms and conditions were only in English—as if, in CHILE, I wouldn’t have the right to a Spanish version! But the worst part was yet to come. review_text: We (3 of us) did the 'O' circuit over christmas 2013. Whilst the scenery is jaw droopingly good, the trails great and the circuit quite easy (we are very experienced hikers) it has not been our best hike by a considerable margin. We unavoidably had to go in the peak season so this is a down side as the W side of the circuit is very busy whilst the the other side (the O) is just plain busy. However overall it was a 4/5 trek. I have marked it for the trekking and not the services. Pros Great scenery Good trails Easy route finding Camp sites and refuges en route Camp sites are reasonably priced Cons Very expensive food-take your own food. Refuge costs at Torres is a rip off $71 for a bed, give it a break! Unsmiling help at most refuge/camp spots Some refuge sites had poor facilities-ie toilets Weather down this part of the world is very intermittent. It ranged from 25c, gale force winds, rains and a Scottish winter white out...all in ten days in summer! Also a note of caution. If you are going in season then don't depend on beds or food at refuges as very often you will have teams of runners or hikers coming up behind you or in front en mass and they will take up all of the facilities. We encountered this but luckily took our own tents (you can hire tents and rent them at the camp sites) and all of our food. Worth the trip but I honestly prefer the treks in Nepal and Europe before this one.

review_text: In san Pedro de Atacama, taking a tour to see the Salar in Bolivia is a must do! During our tour we didn’t got any explanations, our guide was actually just a driver. When we would ask questions about Bolivia or the Salar he would give a quick answer but without making effort to speak Spanish slowly to be understood by everybody. When we would ask a question about him to break the ice, he would answer quickly as well without asking any question in return, not even our names. We never shared a lunch together or even a coffee to get to know each other. If you are just interested in a robotic driver who would take you to the right location to take your pictures, go ! If you want to learn something about the Bolivian culture, the history of the sites you visit, take another tour !

review_text: Valle Nevado was built years ago to attract Braziian tourists. Expect to find a lot of Brazilians there - not a bad thing. VN is like bowl skiing in the US. There are no trees - just completely wide open. Unfortunately there was only a 14 inch base when we were there. We were in Santiago on business and decided to go there for the weekend. Its a 2 hour drive from Santiago. Be careful what time you leave to get there. Its a 2 lane road with 60 hairpin turns going up to an altitude of 3000 meters. For a premium resort which they market as - they made a terrible mistake of adding a sledding facility about 30 minutes away from skiing. The problem with this facility is that many people park along the road to go to this facility and for many families who don't want to go skiing or pay for the sledding facility - they decide to park along the road - bbq and let their kids sled down using garbage bags and mats from their cars. Because its a two lane road - it took an hour just to get through this mess. We got there late and had lunch at the outdoor restaurant - La Inverna or something like that - 2 burgers, water and 2 beers - $50 USD. Really? Is this Aspen? Between the three hotels - tres puntas, valle nevado and Sols - there are many restaurants and the food is not bad. On the skiing front - we didn't have good snow. The resort overall is next to La Parva and another. But, you need to buy a special lift ticket to ski all of them. VN is not that big. The lifts down by the hotels get pretty crowded - Andes Express. We never even made it down to the base lodge where the gondola runs. My bigger complaint - if you are an advanced skier or better - you want to ski the peaks - guess what - no chair lifts. you have to ride poma and t-bars. I haven't ridden one of these since when I was a kid in NY. These lifts are very uncomfortable - have lags and accelerate - putting stress on your arms, thighs. When they accelerate - actually lifted me of the ground and I way 175. My friend fell of the lift - had to ski through ungroomed snow - ended up falling and getting a slight concussion. It was a great experience to ski in July when its summer in the US. Everyone is friendly. IF they want to market themselves as a "premium" resort - fix the roads - get rid of the sledding facility which creates traffic jams and add chairlifts to replace the poma and t-bars at the peaks. Beautiful country - not sure I would go back as a foreigner. Rather stay in US and play golf in the summer and ski Deer Valley and Okemo during our winter.

review_text: The first thing that strikes you as you wander through San Pedro de Atacama is the sheer number of tour agencies - just about every second shopfront is selling tours, and all to the same destinations around the region. Prices vary and from all accounts, you get what you pay for. If you want quality guides, safe drivers, good transport and experiences you'll remember for the right reasons, then expect to pay a little more. We did plenty of TA research when we arrived to work out which agency to explore the area with. Whipala's reviews were consistently good and after visiting their small shopfront on Tocopilla, we signed up for three tours with them. We would have signed up for a fourth but the timing didn't work. We also saved 20% on our tours by paying cash. Our first tour was the Valle de la Luna sunset trip with Philippe as our guide. Philippe was engaging, interesting and enthusiastic from the get-go and explained everything in Spanish and English. The tour visited salt caves (which we conga-lined our way through), the Duna Mayor (a massive sand dune), the Three Mary's rock formations, and finally, Coyote Rock for sunset. As this is probably the most popular tour out of San Pedro, all of the sites were heaving with people and we shared sunset with about a thousand others. Regardless, each site was interesting, the sunset views were spectacular, and Philippe did a fantastic job at explaining the geology and history of the places we visited. Philippe was also our guide for our visit to the El Tatio geysers, which starts in the wee hours in order to get to the geysers for early morning, when they're most active. The initial drive takes around 1hr40 so we slept all the way there. Like Coyote Rock, El Tatio is busy with lots of tour buses but as the site is so large, groups generally have a good amount of distance between them. Again, Philippe's explanations about the location and the geology were excellent - he even used his ipad mini to draw the processes taking place under our feet. Back at our van, an awesome breakfast was waiting for us, including toasted bread, ham, cheese, avocado, scrambled eggs, cake, coffee and tea. From the geyser field, we made our way to the nearby hot springs where a couple of brave souls among us went for a dip (it had started snowing by this stage) and the rest of us wandered the nearby geysers. On our return to San Pedro, we made several stops too see local birdlife, some impressive scenery, and to buy freshly barbecued llama brochettes at the small village of Machuca. Both of our tours with Philippe had around 14 people and we travelled in a new van. Our driver was safe and careful, and we had to wear seatbelts. Our third tour with Whipala was the Red Rocks all-day tour with the charming Rodrigo. This was definitely the highlight of our stay in San Pedro - the landscapes we passed through and visited on this trip were beyond beautiful. We lucked out on this tour as there were just three of us, plus Rodrigo, so we travelled in a 4x4 ute. Rodrigo timed our travels so we arrived at sites ahead of the other vans (though a plus of this tour is that we found the sites visited were nowhere near as busy as the more popular sites). Our first destination was Laguna Chaxa, where we saw several species of flamingo and other high altitude lagoon birds. We ate breakfast here surrounded by mountains - another fabulous spread like the one we had at El Tatio. Our next stop was Laguna Talar/Red Rocks - an absolutely spectacular location with ancient red lava, a milky blue salt lagoon and incredible mountain and volcano views. Our favourite place! We went on to visit the altiplano lagoons of Meñiques and Miscanti, stopped for a three-course lunch in the village of Socaire, and dropped by the village of Toconau to see their church and markets. Throughout the tour, we drove through the most incredible landscapes, spotting vicuña, foxes and birdlife. Rodrigo speaks excellent English and kept us entertained and very well informed all day; he was absolute delight to have as a guide. Thank you to Rodrigo and Philippe for being such awesome guides. We wouldn't hesitate to recommend Whipala and these guys!

review_text: It is very close to the metro station, and it takes no longer than 1 hour to visit the fair, so I would recommend it. Although, my recommendation is that you visit there on a Saturday: there is a fruits and seafood fair between the station and the market which is really worth a visit. He drove us safely to Isla Negra and educated us on the history of the Nobel Peace Prize winners Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda. Isla Negra was stunning. The scenery alone was unforgettable. I can now see why Pablo Neruda felt soo much inspiration and love for this place. His house/museum is incredible and the outdoor gardens overlooking the pacific ocean, gorgeous. Next stop was the worlds largest swimming pool, it's crazy how this was built and how people actually use it. Some people have way too much money, time and are clearly bored. Next was a lovely stop for lunch and the charming city of Pomaire, renowned for their pottery making. Make sure you pick up some good luck three legged clay pigs for your loved ones. Shop around, they are tiny and you will eventually find them. The pottery was of good quality and very inexpensive, perfect place to purchase souvenirs. Overall lovely day tour. review_text: Every year I travel somewhere in the world. This time was Chile. I love the Andes Mountains, the central valley with their exquisite cuisine and wines. I traveled with my sister up and down the coast, stopping in some incredible places, like the summer house that the poet Pablo Neruda kept in the town of Isla Negra. It’s better if you make reservations ahead of time, since school children’s are always present in their field trips. The house now a museum, is just perfect, you can really feel what the poet live like in that serene and peaceful place. The blue ocean, the beautiful garden, and the sunny day with a wonderful temperature were really nice to have your refreshment in the little café, eating the delicious pastries and an aromatic tea. Chileans are so unique in their way to savory their meals, some may skip dinner but never the time for having “onces” or tea service. Going back to Neruda, you can buy the poems book and just read it right there. “I can write the saddest verses tonight”…

review_text: It is a museum that focuses on honoring the memories of the events that lead up to and those lost in the political coup of 1973. This museum is heavy. However it deals with issues like torture and prisoner camps with respect to those who lived through them. As would be expected there is little POV of the military of that time. However, I was amazed by the powerful design and curation of this museum in the sense that it truly allows visitors to experience the different phases of the effects of this coup. Starting with the news reports and film clips prior to and during the coup are shown. The 2nd floor where in darkened hidden alcoves, the devices and methods of torture are documented utilizing many personal accounts form survivors. The 3rd floor is like a release where the art, film, writing and music that inspired by these events are displayed as part of a the countries cultural healing process. I was truly moved.

A tour is recommended, or you need to have a 4WD car and a really good map with some offroad experience. Take (one) the wrong exit(s) and you'll end up in Bolivia without seeing any borders. Careful with the loose sand, which might get you stuck if you're not an experienced driver. However, go there because it's really beautiful!

review_text: The best way to see and appreciate these water eroded marmer rocks is by Kayak and in the early morning. We booked this tour through the hotel El Puesto. In total only 6 persons with the guides. The hotel manager took one tourist in her boat. We were well equipped with a stable double kayak and floating vests. Only the rudder needed repair, but that is no problem when you know how to steer. Only a small distance from the departure point to the two free and one land-attached rock features. The smallest rock is so much eroded at the water level that it can collapse at any moment with a small earthquake. A bit scary. We received a waterproof bag for the camera, but for making pictures you need to take it out of course. The feature is really extraordinary.

review_text: I didn't really know what to expect at Pukara de Quitor, but it was great! The hike at the viewpoint might have been even better than the ruins! Then, you can continue toward Catarpe and bike through Quebrada del Diablo. From there, if you still have time, you can check out some of the other stuff in Catarpe, such as the tunnel, Piedra Achos, y Tambo de Catarpe.

As we trekked in December, there were strong winds and some rain/snow. But once you accepted that, it was a highly rewarding trip. We made the effort to trek up to Torres del Paine lookout for sunrise (despite it dumping with snow overnight). Unfortunately we weren't rewarded with a clear view of the Towers, but the trek was still worthwhile for the experience. Worth the effort!

review_text: We had a fantastic stargazing experience taking the SAT II tour with our guide Jorge! Jorge picked us up at our hotel around 8:30 PM, along with a few other people joining us on our tour, and drove us outside of town to his stargazing spot. First, Jorge gave us a very interesting lecture on the history of Astronomy and explained to us how to use the different types of telescopes he had set up. Although it was cloudy during the day, by the time Jorge had finished his lecture, the clouds began to clear! Next, we had a short break with delicious snacks and hot drinks that his wife had brought out for us. And after this we began the observation session. Jorge had multiple different telescopes set up, and he quickly jumped between them to point them to interesting celestial objects. We saw stars and nebulas in more detail than I've ever seen! Jorge even helped several of us set up our own cameras and tripods to take some long exposure photos with our cameras. Jorge had also set up his own camera right as the Milky Way started to become visible. He took some amazing photos of us looking out into the Milky Way to send to us later. We saw a lot of stars from inside the enclosure, but some of the best views were actually visible when we left the enclosure and saw the open sky without the enclosure walls. After the tour was finished, around 2 AM, Jorge drove all of us back to our hotels. We had such a great time on this tour and would highly recommend it to anyone visiting Atacama!

review_text: Husband and I hiked the W this past February. Due to the Refugio availability we had to keep Torres for the last day. It worked out great as we would have missed the peaks in a cloudy morning on our 1st day. We stayed at El Chileano the night prior to our climb for the sunrise. Woke up at 4 had a quick breakfast with our headlamps on (provided by the lodge with 4 other hikers) before starting on the trail by 4:30. The sky was dark and clear..full of stars as we ascended. The last 30 minutes of the trail was pretty rocky. We got there about 6:30 and waited for sunrise at 7:08 (the lodge wrote down the sunrise time on their board). I got so cold and started to shake. Some people brought their sleeping bag with them and bundled up while waiting - which is smart! It was 7 amazing minutes! The golden shades of dawn kept changing. One of the most beautiful sunrises over mountain peaks I've seen yet. We were grateful that the weather turned out perfect for it.

review_text: We walked around this area many times during a recent visit to Santiago. The plaza is where you can find locals taking casual walks and simply absorbing every ounce of historical architecture in the buildings that line it. Plaza de La Constitucion is located in front of the northern facade of the Palacio de la Moneda and is surrounded by other government buildings such as those housing the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Justice, Banco Central de Chile and the Intendencia de Santiago. Designed by the Italian architect Joaquín Toesca and built in the late 18th century, the Palacio de la Moneda is said to be one of the finest neoclassical buildings in South America. Originally intended as the Royal Mint, today the palace houses the Chilean presidential offices.

Plaza de La Constitucion is located in front of the northern facade of the Palacio de la Moneda and is surrounded by other government buildings such as those housing the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Justice, Banco Central de Chile and the Intendencia de Santiago. Designed by the Italian architect Joaquín Toesca and built in the late 18th century, the Palacio de la Moneda is said to be one of the finest neoclassical buildings in South America. Originally intended as the Royal Mint, today the palace houses the Chilean presidential offices.

review_text: I've been around, probably not as the most seasoned travelers, but nonetheless I have seen a lot of houses. This one is different. The exterior is not particularly noteworthy, but the interior is what you are there for. This can be an emotional experience (it was for me) because Neruda in his wisdom made a house out of love. The house is about memories, not for the sake of producing melancholy, but rather because he wanted to extend his childhood play and friendship tributes well into his old years. The house is about all we endear: infancy, friends, food, drinks, time. And it's of course facing the Ocean. You have to see the master bedroom and the spectacular view that it affords towards the waters. A tip: the restaurant next to the house is excellent and relatively affordable. Make reservations on time if you are visiting in a weekend. They run out of tickets. We got the last tickets of the day when we arrived shortly after noon on a Saturday.

review_text: Just like other reviewers, we also rented bikes in San Pedro. It is a great way of exploring the area. You can drive directly from the center or come from the Death/Mars Valley through a shortcut (like we did). After passing Pukara de Quitor, you will reach a gate where you need to sign in a book and pay the entrance fee. Also you can get a map and directions. The Devil's Gorge is only one of the several things you can see in the area, also the tunnel and Cuchabrache are included, for example. I wished we would have known this, perhaps we could have arrived earlier and done more exploring. After driving straight for a while, there will be a sign to turn right to the Devil's Gorge. It is an impressive area of rock formations. It feels like a labyrinth with high walls. However, it is easy to navigate if you stay on the main road, but you can also explore in all directions. You have to carry the bike on two occasions, but it is possible to drive to the end. We opted for walking the second half, which was a different and more intensive experience. (Cycling is more fun during the first half, while the path is more narrow.) The end of the route is clearly marked. I guess you can still continue and do a loop, but for us it was safer to return on the same path. Before doing so, we climbed up the hill to a viewpoint - it was impressive to see everything from above. It was a fun way of discovering the area and seeing some of the characteristic rock formations. The bike trip is not too difficult if you have at least average fitness, though it can be strenuous at times because of the heat and the road conditions.

review_text: We were lucky to be there during low season so my husband and I got our guide to ourselves. Cristian was the best guide we could have hoped for! He was so friendly, professional yet humble (which is not easy to find in a wine expert!) and very knowledgeable. We decided to do a tour, tasting and make-your-own-wine experience. We started off by walking around outside. At this point it was our 3rd winery we visited in Chile so I didn't think it would be so different. Boy was I wrong! We learned lots of interesting facts we hadn't heard before. Cristian was very entertaining and can answer any question we had with so many details yet make it 'dumbed down' enough for us to understand everything. Talented guide! The tour was super interesting. We then past on to the tasting part. Because it was low season, we got a big of a special treatment! Some important people had been over the night before or something and long story short, they opened every bottle they had and so there were left overs of anything we wanted to try! We tried 6 of their best wines (and didn't pay extra for any of it), 'el filete' he called it ('the steak')...the best of the best. They accompanied it with delicious pairings, too! None of the other wineries had done any of this. It was important for me that he be a part of the tasting by joining us as I felt wine should be enjoyed in a social ambient where he can tell us what he is tasting right then and there and we can do the same. It was so much fun! I took a photo of my favorites, made a couple of mental notes and concluded the tasting part of the tour. Now came the last part: making our own wines! A little tipsy (I hadn't spit any of the wine), we made our way downstairs to the basement where we would combine different types of red wine to percentages we liked. We already knew all the properties of each wine and what we liked best so the rest was just a bit of trial and error with some great reserve wines they had (Merlot, Carmenère and Cabarnet Sauvignon) and voilà!! We bottled it, corked it, sealed it, and labelled it! We then bought a bottle of one that I knew before hand I couldn't get my hands on in Canada (check online before coming!) and happily left (husband drove, plan ahead!). The make-your-own wine experience is touristy, yes..but it's so much fun! What made the experience so special was our guide, Cristian. The tour was so informative and thorough and most importantly: not pretentious!

review_text: A visit to the El Tatio Geysers is consider one of the three 'quintessential' tours of San Pedro - the others being the Altiplano lakes and Valle de la Luna. Standard tours begin at 0400 aiming to arrive at sunrise as to have the largest temperature difference between geyser vs air and therefore the most steam. The tours usually take 90 minutes to get to El Tatio and it's 64 Geysers (3rd highest number in the world) and then stop at a hot spring before meandering back via a scenic road featuring local wildlife (flamingoes, vicunas) and a stop at Machucha village before returning to San Pedro at around 1300. I completed this trip with my partner in November 2015 and here are a few tips for those considering visiting here. (1) Go WITH A SMALLER TOUR COMPANY - This is really the only thing you need to consider when booking a tour. All the companies follow the exact same itinerary and serve almost identical breakfasts. Generally the guides all speak decent English and their main function is as a transport service. The key thing with a smaller tour company is that you don't spend 1.5 hours like we did with our company (Latchir) driving around San Pedro De Atacama picking everyone up (as half of them sleep through their alarms). Words can't describe how annoying this time wastage is after waking up at 0400am. Tours all cost around the same - 20000CP per person but this doesn't include the 5000CP ticket entry price. (2) YOU COULD ATTEMPT THIS YOURSELF - Although you would need to hire a decent hire car with some sort of 4x4 capacity as the roads are gravel and not clearly marked. I wouldn't worry too much about directions - you could just follow the cavalcade of tour buses which leave san pedro at around 0500. (3) PACK FOR COLD - The temperature at dawn is between -15 and -5 degrees due to it's high altitude of 4200m. I wore thermals and was still cold. Pack in layers as it subsequently heats up during the day (4) BRING SWIMMERS AND A TOWEL - that's if you want to go in the hot springs. Personally I wouldn't recommend it as it gets pretty crowded and the outside temperature is pretty cold. (5) BRING SUNSCREEN + WATER - Don't worry about food as breakfast should be included. You can buy llama sticks and/or empanadas at Machucha village. What was my thoughts of the tour? To be honest - I was a bit underwhelmed. Although there are 64 geysers in the field they're pretty small and the crowds of tourists (~200) become quite oppressive. The biggest problem is they all arrive at exactly the same time and follow the exact same itinerary so you are constantly swamped. Most importantly if you are doing the Uyuni salt flats tour (ie going San Pedro > Uyuni or the other way) you stop at the high altitude geysers on the 1st day (or 3rd if you are travelling towards SPDA) - these are just as impressive and feature far less crowds than El Tatio. I personally would recommend holding out for these if you are doing the tour and saving your money unless you are Geyser-mad. Please take the time to rate my review

review_text: Jose was very responsive from the first contact. Other kayak companies capped their ages for the tour at 65, I am 68 and my partner is 70, we are still very active but that age limit seemed daunting. Jose was very definite about that not being an issue. As our trip date approached, Jose contacted us to put back the trip a couple of days due to bad weather. The day of our full day Gray River trip, the crew picked us up in Puerto Natales and with a trailer full of boats and gear we headed to Torres del Paine. Jose gave us an orientation and we suited up in dry suits, pogies, and pfds. The equipment was all in very good shape and the crew assisted us into the kayaks. We headed down the Gray River with amazing views of the mountains. Jose and the other two guides were always around keeping an eye on things but not interfering with your enjoyment of the river. And when the wind became a factor in certain sections, they were ready to assist. I was really impressed when in one section full of shallows and tree snags in the current, Jose and the guides were ready to connect a tow rope and navigate through the correct channel. We had a delicious riverside lunch and continued down the river to the take out, which almost seemed too soon. It was a memorable day and a way to see the park like none other.

review_text: What a wonderful surprise this excursion was from NCL. A short trip through the village brought us to this Park. After donning large yellow ponchos and collecting a water at the visitor center, our guide led through this beautiful rainforest. The foliage was dense and rich green, the birds were singing and the mud was walkable. Our guide stopped and explained certain plants, flowers, mushrooms and moss. Some plant leaves were as big as me, and some mushrooms looked like white fingers sticking out of the trees! The two highlights of our hike were the thundering waterfall and the two large ring-necked kingfishers. Beautiful area of the wet Patagonia. We ended our hike with a roasted lamb meal at a circular windowed building up the hill overlooking a lake. Great view to enjoy a delicious meal.

review_text: We went here today originally hoping to do the more difficult hike to the summit (Andino, I think it's called) but accidentally went to the wrong entrance. The guides did say you need to be there by 9:30am, though, so that's something to keep in mind. Instead we did a 7km hike to Ocoa, I can't remember what the name was. The hike up, due to constant uphill and hot temperatures was relatively difficult. Definitely doable by almost any fitness level but the path could be difficult for those with bad knees. It took us just under 2 hours to the top, where we had lunch, and then another 1.5 hours downhill. The park estimates 4 hours total, so that was true for us but we went quite fast so maybe add some time to your estimate if you don't hike a lot or aren't of at least moderate fitness. While it wasn't an amazing hike, it was fun and enjoyable. A good portion of it is fully exposed to sun though, so make sure to bring a hat and sunscreen. We didn't have any issues with bugs along the hike but there were a bunch of bees at the top. No problems from them, though.

review_text: I can't convey in this review what a wonderful day we had with Mauricio. It started when he picked us up at our hotel. He is so nice and fun and well-informed. We began our day with a tour of Santiago-- from the surrounding hills for the views to the old town for the history. Along the way, we learned all about the history of both Santiago and Chile in a fun and fascinating way. We never asked a question he couldn't answer. He is well-educated and passionate about what he does-- which is to make visitors to Chile learn about his amazing country and understand Chile's amazing history. From Santiago, we headed to the wine country-- Casablanca. We had left all of the details of the day to Mauricio so we really didn't know what to expect -- but what a wonderful surprise. We started at a lovely vineyard and restaurant where Mauricio worked with the chef to do a special 4 course lunch with wine pairings just for us. Not only is he a tour guide-- but a gourmet and a wine aficionado in every respect. We learned so much and we had a wonderful lunch in a fabulous setting. From there, we visited one more vineyard with some red wines scoring 95. If you are looking for a wonderful tour combining both Santiago's history with a fabulous lunch and wine tour, this is the trip I would recommend. My husband and i travel all over the world, but I am hard pressed to remember such a fun, interesting and lovely day as the day we just spent with Chilean Wine Lovers and Mauricio. Gracias!

review_text: The many positive reviews of Mercado de Chillan must have been written by people who have never visited a market before. We have visited markets all over the world, and Chillan's market must qualify as one of the smallest and most boring. There is a small section with both handmade and industrially produced handicrafts, but it does not differ much from all the tourist junk you can buy everywhere. The food section of the market caters to the locals, who apparently are not too spoiled. A Frenchman or an Arab would leave here furious - no delicacies, no refinement, everything sloppily presented. That this market is one of Chillan's tourist attractions says a lot about what else the city has to offer.

review_text: Fantastic cultural day spent on 3 Mapuchi estancias. Our guide Catalina was excellent, friendly and professional. The first was self sufficient and had cows, sheep, chickens and a wild, overgrown vegetable area. Some of the animals were sold including the fleece to get an income. Magaly was a very humble and sweet natured lady who taught us a lot about the herbs she plants in the fields to keep the animals healthy. The second visit to Juanita's vegetable farm was completely different. This was run as a business and everything was very organised. Her products were sold at market every Friday. She was constantly busy running a huge area by herself (with a little help from her daughter), whilst her husband looked after the sheep. We had a lovely drink and snack here, which we actually thought was our lunch. Our third farm was again vegetables but also ran as a homestay and they were collecting entrance fees to a short trek to a view point to see the Villarrica Volcano. Here we learnt how to roast wheat over a fire, grind it and make wheat coffee, which is only made by the Mapuchi people. Rosita cooked the best lamb lunch that we had had on our two month trip! Definitely worth the visit.

review_text: I would recommend, if you have the time and can arrange the transportation, taking the hike to Glacier Grey then catch the boat back. The hike is not strenuous, there is little elevation gain, but it is 3-6 miles depending on how close you hike to the glacier. Be aware of the boat's schedule and plan your pick-up time accordingly. It's best to pack a lunch & bring water. Allow an entire day for the hike so that the walk through the lovely beech forest and the spectacular viewpoints can be leisurely enjoyed. The wind off the glacier can be strong and cold so bring a windbreaker and fleece or wool shirt. Condors are usually seen riding the thermals above the lake. The earlier comments about the $135 charge to enter Chile through the Santiago airport needs some explaining. The charge is a reciprocity fee implemented by the Chilean government after the US began charging Chileans a fee to enter the US.

review_text: I was in Chile for 3 days and really wanted to see the Andes Mountains up close. This is the perfect tour to do it. The tour is about 8 hours in total, since it takes about 90 min-2 hours to get back with traffic. But the bus was comfortable and our driver Francisco was great. I still don't know how he managed to handle all those winding roads! We stopped on the way there for some complimentary wine and cheese at a cute little restaurant (I think the name is Albonico), then headed our scenic way up the Andes to a height of 8000 ft (2500 meters). The views from the bus are amazing, but when we reached the glaciers and Cajon del Maipo by the lagoon, I instantly was grateful I chose this tour. It's rare to find such majestic natural beauty on earth. Bring warm clothes! We spent an hour exploring the area on our own and taking pictures before heading down and getting a nice lunch and then heading back to the city. Our guide, Jaime Fuenzalida, taught me a lot and was very pleasant and accommodating, as not all guests spoke the same language. I really enjoyed this excursion and I would recommend it to anyone who loves mountains and beautiful views.

review_text: This observatory cost only $3.500 pesos which is about $7 if you have your own transportation and can follow the tour guide's van. We went up about 8:30 from nearby Vicuna, Chile in the Elqui Valley. Then, inside the dome they had a couple of short videos projected on the walls using a computer. They showed how the stars looked that night and, say, 50 years ago. It's all in Spanish. Then, they took our group outside to see the stars. Fortunately, we had a relatively clear night so many stars were visible. Our guide used a laser to point out the important constellations and planets. Then, he pointed the telescope toward various objects such as Saturn, Arcturas, the Tarantula Nebula, etc. and allowed all of us (about a dozen in our group) to look one by one. There are better telescopes / observatories in Chile than Mamalluca but the one in El Panque cost ten times as much and they didn't have enough people that night to confirm that we could go. Still, I know you get what you pay for, but the Mamalluca was worth more than the $7 apiece we spent. We had a nice time and saw a couple of "shooting stars" to boot. We don't get to see the Southern Cross in the northern Hemisphere so that was a bonus. The guide reminded us that the ancient mariners used the Southern Cross to navigate centuries ago.

review_text: My wife and I stayed from December 22, 2016 through January 12, 2017 in a wonderful hotel located across the street from Park Forestal. Our room on the 4th floor had a balcony overlooking the park. This is a beautiful park with lovely green grass, many monuments, fountains, children's play areas, and lots of beautiful trees. The caretakers in the park water the grass early every morning for a couple of hours. There are delightful wide walkways made of chat throughout the park and lots and lots of benches. The park is very safe and we saw people roaming through the park at midnight. In the afternoons and early evening, there are often musicians playing in the park hoping for appreciative tips. There was even an acrobat on Sunday afternoons entertaining the crowd by acrobatics on long wide fabrics hanging from trees. The park is not wide but it is very long. It is obviously a place for lovers lounging, talking a making out on the grass in the park every afternoon and evening. It was also a great place for dogs (lots of them) running around and being walked by owners. Children were also everywhere on the playgrounds, chasing each other, and riding bikes. It is a place for families, couples and others looking for a place to have a nice rest. It was fun to watch and enjoy the green space.

review_text: I’m a huge fan of Cabernet Sauvignon wine and Chilean wines are my typical go to. It’s been in my bucket list to visit the vineyards of Chile and thanks to Colchagua wine tours I and my wife were able to experience some beautiful vineyard tours with tastings Connie coordinated with me asking me my interests and where my wife and I were and n Chile. I let her know we were staying in Santiago and requested visiting some staple medium sized(when compared to vinyards like Conca y Toro and Santa Rita) very excellent vineyards (Viu Manet, Maquis, and Neyen plus lunch at a fourth great vineyard (Montes). She organized a driver to pick us up at 8am, drive us to all the locations and drop us back off in Santiago at 8pm. Our driver Victor was on time, very friendly and an excellent driver on the road. Viu Manet was great, our English speaking guide Sophia was well informed, able to answer all our questions and welcoming. We were able to taste several wines including 2 ICON wines (ICON wines are the highest level of wine quality that a vineyard produces) and theses did not disappoint. Maquis vineyard, our second stop, was interesting as they are forward thinking in terms on preserving the environment and pesticide alternatives. The good humored guide (Pablo) took us on a nature walk of the grounds and then a great tasting. Third stop was fuegos de alpata restaurant located on the Montes winery. I don’t consider myself a “foodie” but as someone who regularly cooks and bakes I know when food is of high caliber and this was PHENOMENAL! We also drank glasses of the vineyard”s wine while enjoying our food. Finally we went to Neyen vineyard which did a “vertical tasting” meaning multiple bottles of different years of the same wine, the purpose to see how the flavor/notes of the wine change over time. It was a type of tasting I had not done before and found it very informative. As promised we were back in Santiago by 8 pm. My wife and I enjoyed the experience completely and are grateful to Connie and her team at colchagua tours.

review_text: Always use HOHO buses when exploring new cities. Bought our tickets in UK via expeadia as it was cheaper. On ticket it said to board at any stop and present ticket. No problem that’s what we’ve always done So at 9.30 we get on at stop 8. No sign to say bus stops here but fortunately we’d seen it stop there the previous day. The lovely driver who spoke no English explained via signs and gestures that we needed a wristband. So we got on at stop 8 and off at 10 to get our wrist band from the fourth floor in the Sky Tower. No signage to explain where to go! Got wristband from young guy who spoke no English ( you need your passport too!) and decided to go up the tower before getting back on bus. He had to google ground floor to tell us where to enter the Tower We then rejoined bus. No signage to say where it stopped but we knew because we’d got off there. review_text: I totally recommend taking the bike tour of pretty Vina Cousino Macul. I was in a group of just two with Chris, our very amiable and articulate guide from ‘La bicicleta verde’. We were able to get out into the vineyard, away from the busier ‘on-foot’ tours, and could take in the scenery and the serenity of the location. After a lovely ride and wine tasting in the vineyard, Chris took us back to the bodega to cool down in underground cellars while he explained the antique production process, and todays’s more efficient, but less picturesque, process. After this we tasted three more wines while Chris explained the intricacies and subtleties of really experiencing the wine. Even my dull palette was able to discern the differences! The whole experience felt like a privilege. It is also as easy trip from downtown Santiago on the metro to Quilin and a very nice walk passed some amazing street art on the walls of the park before the vineyard. Gracias Chris and Cousino Macul for a unique experience!
