review_text: I booked a day trip to Valle Nevado months in advance since I had a long flight layover in Santiago and wanted to check out the resort. Ski Total is one of a few options to get there from Santiago as there is no public transportation and renting a vehicle may be a hassle, particularly because you may need a 4x4 or tyre chains. So I contacted the company by email. Pedro, the boss, was very responsive as we went back and forth to finalize the details of the itinerary. Unfortunately there was no snow but although I had the option to cancel and not get charged until the day prior, I decided to keep the trip. Something worth considering if you plan to get to Valle for a day trip, like I did, is that it looks deceivingly close but it may be a long trip. I landed at 9:15 and was on the slopes at 12 noon, which is great, but it was under ideal conditions: only passenger, no need to rent gear, no traffic, perfect weather. It might take much longer when the resort is open for skiing because traffic gets intense on the small road to the resort, which has 60 switchbacks! It also sometimes gets shut down if there is heavy snow. And you have to add the time to rent the gear at the Ski Total shop in Santiago. All in all it may take 4-6 hrs to get to the slopes, according to the locals. So either leave from Santiago very early by choosing a flight that arrives before 8 am or you may risk to get to the resort in the late afternoon. As far as Ski Total is concerned, my driver Arturo was very friendly and professional and the ride was great. I will use this company again in the future.

review_text: Chimanga en Patagonia was a great experience for me. I stayed there for several days and enjoyed the hospitality of Juan. There are a lot of activitys to do. review_text: Our apartment was located in Bellavista, so the choice of city tours was very convenient. The agent who booked our 3 tours, by the name of Franco, was very knowledgeable and spoke excellent English. I must say that all of the Turistik guides/agents spoke English and we were impressed by the seamless transfer system they use to get us to and from the various meeting points. The drivers all deserve medals for their expertise in getting us to pour destinations swiftly and safely as well. Being seniors, my husband and I opted for the 2-day tour, to get our bearings and to know where to hop off the next day. The start-off point was #3 for us, and we decided to complete the morning tour and go past the first stop to # 2 in order to get us onto the gondola/teleferico up the mountain and then the funicular back down to our stop at the foot of San Cristobal Hill. We found that the large shopping mall at Parque Arauco was a good place for a short stop and lunch and is where most of the transfers take place. Just before each stop, a guide announced the next stop to passengers on the upper deck of the bus as well as those downstairs, in enough time to get off if required. We had an enjoyable ride up and down the mountain, enjoying the spectacular views and spent some time at the top, walking partly up to the statue (it's quite a hike to the top!) but the view was absolutely worth it. Good footwear is definitely recommended! The ID bracelet we wore for the 2 days gave us a seamless experience with boarding and transfers and we found that the personnel both from the tour company and the gondola or funicular were very efficient and friendly. On the second day, we took the bus for a few stops and got off downtown and walked the rest of the way, now that we knew in which direction to turn and were able to visit or take photos of the many points of interest along the way. That was money and time well-spent in our opinion and we recommend this tour to any new visitor to Santiago. Para nosotros es muy importante conocer las apreciaciones de nuestros queridos viajeros, cariñosos visitantes. Nos llena de alegría saber que formamos parte de sus lindos recuerdos por Chile. Estaremos ansiosos esperando su retorno. ¡Un abrazo!

review_text: Located next to Universidad Católica Metro Station, this center is usually worth a visit not only because of its innovative copper and wooden architecture but also because of the great expositions and cultural events that use to take place there. Chile Monos was actually a very good example of it, as it showed a very complete graphic sample of the whole history of chilean cartoons, so it was very interesting to get to know all those kinds of styles of cartoons over the years, and to see how have them diversified lately also with the help of technology. I was really impressed that there were so much cartoons and that some of them were really high quality, as I definitely wasn't aware that Chile was that developed in that area. The sample included a special place both for the chilean winner of the 2017's Academy Award for the best Animated Short Film, and for the first chilean cartoon. There you can watch some videos about these latest. I only missed there weren't more about the other cartoons, but I definitely recommend a visit anyway!

review_text: My wife and I visited Humberstone and Santa Laura in December 2010 with our English-speaking Guide, Rudi. Humberstone is a ghost town where the saltpeter miners lived; it has been designated as a cultural heritage museum and there is a small fee to enter. The place has been abandoned since 1960 but much of the location dates back before 1900. There is a huge theater that is still in good condition, a bakery, an ice plant, offices, and a riveter iron swimming pool! Santa Laura, just across the road about a half- mile, lies completely abandoned-- just walk in and wander around in the old steel & wood buildings. There is a huge nitrate processing plant with a tall smokestack, a building housing two old two-cylinder engines (made in England) that generated electricity for the plant, and a building with 4 or 5 old air compressors. It is spooky to listento the old corrugated tin buildings rattling and banging in the wind-- it is a perfect movie location. Chile exported nitrate and earned fabulous wealth until a synthetic process (the Haber Process) for making ammonia was developed in Germany in the 1920s. The market for Chilean nitrate plummeted but smaller minimg operations continued until it shut down completely in 1960. Consider driving to Santa Laura & Humberstone on the way from Iquique to the oasis of Pica.

review_text: This artisans village is definitely worth the trip. It's an easy 5 minute walk from the nearest underground station (which is the end of the line) and therefore easy to get to. The village itself is a set of old colonial style buildings, each of which is converted into a little shop. All of the shops sell hand crafted items of various different descriptions. There is wood craft, metal work, leather work, alpaca wool products, jewellery, painting, ceramics and household goods, as well as food and a small restaurant. The prices are reasonable for the most part, some things more expensive, and others quite cheap. I found that it was a little more expensive than some of the street stalls I had come across, but far cheaper than tourist shops and the airport. Keep in mind any quarantine laws your country might have, but this is a great place for a little shopping!

After that, I went to their office and very respectfully and calmly expressed my obeservations and the lady apologized, seemed to listen and assured me this was an exception. Next day, I did two tours, the first one to Tatio, it was about an hour shorter than announced but otherwise ok. In the afternoon, I did the tour of Valle de la Luna. Here, I had explicitly asked whether it was possible to pick me up at my hostel instead of meeting at the agency, as online in the description this was explained as a choice one could make. At pick up time the tour guide called me asking me where I was and telling me generally all tour in the afternoon start from agencies only, there must have been a "misunderstanding" (later asked other agencies and as a matter of fact, all afternoon tours start in the village and there is no pcik up, so the lady completely lied to me knowing it was going to be a problem, I guess because I had caught them on their little "chofer as guide"-action. We where supposed to se the sunset over Valle de Muerte, but once the sun was disappearing and the pretty light effects we came for started we were called and had to go, left a lot earlier than 90% of the other tours and therefore couldn't actually do what was announced in the description, visit to Valle de la Luna beforehand was also extremely short. Tour guide had the audacity to ask for tips after very obviously doing the bare minimum and also grunting very aggressively at a fellow traveller who had "dared" to ask him why we hadn't received the pisco sour cocktail the tour guide kept announcing over and over during the tour. Also, apart from the big fails like sending us to a tour without guide and intentionally shortening tours, also in the little things they seem to be in it for the money: breakfast, lunch and afternoon snacks are of low quality compared to other agencies, they use paper and plastic cups were other agencies have switched to reusable cups etc. etc. After this awful afternoon tour I felt quite cheated and went back to their office requesting explanation and a compensation. review_text: Everything, absolutely everything in this park is breathtaking. Every view, every walk. It is spectacular beauty. It's hard to believe that a place like this exists in real life. Absolutely, 100%, go. We went in the off season. Honestly, it wasn't that cold. It was in the 30s the entire time we were in Patagonia; like a mild New England winter. I talked to a CONAF employee, and she said that the off season is actually the best season for picture taking because the mountains are snowy and gorgeous, and the fierce Patagonian winds are at their mildest. Don't shy away from going in the Chilean winter! The park never closes, but in the off season, hiking access to some of the trails are limited. The park rangers decide on a day to day basis what trails will be open and which ones will be closed or restricted. CONAF publishes a report on the status of all of the trails at approximately 9:00/9:30 each morning. We weren't able to hike to the base of the towers, as the trail didn't open the entire week we were there. Remember that, although the daily busses to the park don't stop in the off season, they run on very limited schedules, and if you plan on hiking one of the more difficult trails, your best bet is to get there by a rented car (check the status of the roads before you go). Because we couldn't hike to the base of the towers, we chose to visit the park in a day tour. We went with Laguna Azul, a wonderful tour company! The tour was reasonably priced, and the company went above and beyond for us when we were stuck without a bus in Puerto Natales. The driver was wonderfully skilled on difficult roads, and the tour guide was knowledgable, efficient, and fun. We left Punta Arenas early in the morning, saw all of the attractions in the park, all more beautiful than the last, and, to maximize our time, requested that they drop us off in Puerto Natales on the way back. It was an incredible, emotional day that we will treasure forever!

review_text: We booked through this agency for a day trip to Geometricas and the following day a trip up to the Volcano. The french delegation are very friendly, the guides were fab for the volcano. I'll start with the Geometricas.. Aguaventura basically subcontracted this out- had nothing to do with them. Felt the price was VERY steep - $35K. We were told by them the bus ride out would be about an hour and 15 min. - in actual fact it was closer to 2.5 hours. (would have been nice to know in advance). So we had 3 hours in the pools. They also said to bring a lunch if we wanted - but there was food there. We were not told, however that you are not allowed to EAT your lunch there. This would also have been nice to know. Geometricas itself was a fab place, no complaints but it's a bit of a trek getting there. We did mention this to one of the guys there and he seemed to genuinely care. Villaricca - this they said they ran from start to finish and for the same price is much more bang for your buck $47K includes all technical gear, expert guides. They kept a good pace matched with our group of about 24 - and took breaks regularly enough. My only minor comment here is that no one every mentioned the difficulty of the climb, one's ability, etc. It's assumed that if you want to climb a volcano, you know what you're in for. The ski lift was not working, so we had no choice but to walk the extra hour up hill - it took us almost 6 hours to get to the top and it's a tough climb. You'd better be in decent if not good shape. Sadly, we got to the top and the crater was covered in cloud - our weather was not the best. I think the badge of honor is really in just making it to the top. The butt sliding back down was good fun - the views are stunning. It could be a somewhat dangerous climb for some - but again, there were enough guides that a few people from our group returned early - and there was a guide to take them down. Would recommend the Volcano trip with these guys - they rock. But know what you're getting in to!!!

review_text: Went to the Eastern side of the park near Pedro de Valdivia Nte & El Cerro and took the cable car. Lots of park guides who speak good english. Paid for a two stop ticket. Got off at the first stop and had a quick look at a little fort. Then back on the cable car to the top. Makes you appreciate the height and distance and glad to take a cable car. Spectacular views of the city from the top with the statue, church and lots of cafes and souvenir shops. Can take the funicular down but decided to walk as it is all downhill. Takes around 45 minutes to walk down but there is a slightly quicker path where the picnic/barbecue area is. Beware of other 'paths' which are actually dedicated cycle paths for nutters on mountain bikes.

review_text: I took the 3pm tour on Wednesday 14 November. Our guide gave a tip estimate of around 12,000 CLP per person. There were a number of indicators that this self-identified "sociologist" had completed very little postgraduate training in his claimed discipline. It began with a promise to separate "fact" from "opinion". Santiago's population size was offered as truth versus (what turned out to be) an inaccurate guess. The Mapuche situation was described in a homogenising, nationalistic manner. The guide was, however, incredibly enthusiastic about Chile 1973 to 1990. And he assisted in obtaining, and gave clear instructions on using, a Bip card. If all you require is the latter, this tour is exactly what you are looking for.

review_text: We were recommended Michael by an American friend. We went by curiosity and we were amazed! A tour of Valparaiso with Mike is not a tour it's a voyage in time and a fantastic human experience Michael is indeed an amazing and down to earth German guy who knows all the little secrets of Valparaiso. Then , Michael takes a glass on a barrel and invites you to taste this Jägermeister like elixir. Fantastic! Did I mantion Michael was German? A few minutes later you feel again in a time machine when you enter a grocery store that welcomed immigrants a century ago. Whenever you enter a shop or a gallery with Michael, the owner greets Michael like a real friend and you feel then very special , like a friend of a friend . When I told to Michael's friend who guards the place that I was French , he started to sing a famous French song : "Alouette , gentille Alouette..." We had à real blast! I highly recommend this tour to anyone who wants to discover Valparaiso like a local and not like a simple tourist . Review of: Discover the treasures of Valparaiso with a local

review_text: We arranged a tour with Carola and she was easy to communicate with throughout our planning stage, however, we did not meet her, as she often subcontracts with another guide, Luis, who was unaware of our hotel change or change of plans. He picked us up promptly at the airport with a sign in hand making it very easy to identify him from the throng of people waiting in this area, which was very nice. We then went to the hotel and dropped off our luggage and went off for our day tour of Santiago. This tour was just ok, but the pace seemed a bit too slow for us and although it had it's moments, those are displaced by our constant standing out in the hot sun and our sweltering, having to constantly remind Luis to move to a shady area (which was always available) when he would lecture us on different aspects of the area. Later on we did a nice walk using our GPSmycity app and enjoyed that walk much more than our day spent with Luis. The next day we planned to visit the Alps with Luis and he arrived 10 minutes late to our hotel. We had rushed to get ready on time and did not appreciate this, but from this point on, we greatly enjoyed our day with him today. He went above and beyond to ensure that we had a very nice time today and this day was a highlight among a trip that are full of wonderful highlights. Highly recommend this day with Luis. He took us to several points within the Alps, we saw wild horses, crossed the river to take some amazing photos on the other side of the river, used his all drive vehicle in order to reach a nice waterfall for us to enjoy a lunch with wine that he prepared for us and even made a few interesting stops along the way. This day deserves 5 full stars! We would highly recommend doing this full day trip to the Alps with Luis. Other reviewers seem to enjoy the Santiago day tour with him as well, but for us, we wouldn't as highly recommend that one. We paid $220 for the Alps tour, and $170 for the airport pick up and Santiago tour and were driven to the tallest building in South America and were going to go to the top and enjoy the views, but declined paying what amounted to an additional $75 to ride the elevator up. That was off-putting and disappointing for us, but it was interesting to just go into this building. I'll include some photos from each tour. Thank you for your comments. review_text: Patagonia and Torres del Paine was a life long dream and living in Scotland meant that it was no easy place to get to. The cheapest flights I could find was a trip from Glasgow to New York, New York to Houston/Texas, Houston to Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires to Santiago/Chile, Santiago Chile to Punta Arenas/Chile. The total flight time was 27.5h. Punta Arenas is a town next to the Strait of Malagan and I loved the colourful wooden houses and the friendly people, who I met when I explored the city.I only stayed for a day, as the Trek I had planned, in the famous Torres del Paine National Park, was still a 5h bus journey away. The hostel had helped me to book a bus ticket to Puerto Natales (closest town to the park) and after a 3h bus journey I was finally at my destination. In the town most of the Hostels and many shops rent out all sorts of equipment and in a number of outdoor stores you can buy what ever you need. I had taken most gear with me from home and to rent a pair of walking poles for 6 days set me back 10 Pounds (not bad). The Erratic Rock Hostel in Punta Arenas arranged a daily information talk in the Base Camp Pub next door and useful information incl. were you should not drink water from the streams were given out over a relaxing cup of tea, coffee or a pint. Camping or Refugios The Trek itself can be done via a Tour Company (the easiest) or by organising everything yourself. I opted for the latter as it is the most cost effective way. The first question you should ask yourself, is if you want to camp or stay in basic accommodation (Refugios). If you want to camp you can either carry all your camping gear, or rent it is the park. Please be aware that wild camping is strictly forbidden, as well as making a fire. You will have to camp in the designated camping areas (between free and 10 Pounds a night) and most have toilets, bathrooms with showers and kitchen areas. Prepared food can be bought in the Refugios (around 25 Pounds for Breakfast, Lunch and dinner) or you buy your food before hand and carry it. If you want to stay in the Refugios you will have to book ahead of time. I booked 4 months in advance and one place was already booked out! So do it at least half a year in advance, if you want to have a warm comfortable bed. Rooms usually have 8 beds and were a lot better than I had imagined. The W, O or Q Trek The 2 main treks people do are the W or O Trek. Simply called W and O by the shape you walk it. The O trek requires you to carry your own tent and camping equipment , as a few places do not have Refugios and only designated camping areas with basic toilets. The W covers the most stunning parts of the walk and the W allows you to choose Refugios or campsites. I opted for the W Trek starting from Lago Grey (anticlockwise) and finish at the famous Torres. The Trek Day 1 Having stayed the day and night in Pueto Natales, I had managed to book the bus to the park, buy enough food to last me for 6 days and pack my backpack. My first day started with an early rise and an hour journey to the Park Entrance. Having paid my entrance fee, together with lots of other people, everyone had to watch a information programme and were reminded that causing a fire can result in a 20 year prison sentence. Harsh, but a few years ago a backpacker caused a wildfire which burned down a huge area of the park, so it made sense. Afterwards everyone was moved back to the bus for another hours travel to the Catamaran to cross Pehoé Lake. The bus arrived with an hour to spare and apart from waiting around, I made the short walk to Salto Grande an impressive waterfall. Having spend far too much time at the fall I nearly missed the boat - ups. Safely on board the trip over the lake was stunning. Ahead the 'Horns' were poking out of the clouds and the fact I was finally in Patagonia sank in. Soon the 45min journey came to an end and I stood in front of Refugio Paine Grande were the walk started and I would return to on day 2. I set off and soon the full weight of my 16 kilo backpack started to show. I was glad for my walking poles, but my hips and legs were struggling with the unfamiliar weight. The path lead up a slight slope through the burned down country side (due to the huge fire caused by the backpacker) and apart from the burned down trees, the countryside reminded me strongly about Scotland. 2 hours into the walk a lake came into view and on were 'Icebergs'. Wow Wow Wow! I stood there for a good ten minutes amazed and excited...I had not expected that. The path lead up a small hill and from the top the edge of Glacier Grey could be seen. A glacier ending in a lake must be one of the most impressive sights on earth and the big grin on my face stayed until I reached the lovely Refugio Grey. The rooms were clean and warm with amazing comfortable beds. I dumped my backpack and headed into the shower, had some food and chatted to a few other walkers I had met during the walk. The days in December are long up to 18h of sunlight in winter time and together with one of my friends, I went for a walk down to the lake edge. On the water a big Iceberg could be seen not far away and along the shore were hundreds of broken off peaces of ice which were floating in the ice cold water. So 'cool' Day 2 Due to the fact that only a short 4h day lay ahead of me, I had decided to take a 3h kayaking trip on Lago Grey. The cost of the trip included full equipment and a short lesson of how to kayak. I was joined up with another unexperienced woman in one kayak, but we managed fine and had a marvellous time kayaking around the glacier. We were so lucky when right in front of us (yet in save distance) 2 huge peaces of the ice broke off and crashed into the water. The sound of it I will never forget and the short walking trip right to the edge close the most compacted ice which appears dark blue was definitely one of the highlights of the trip. After the kayaking trip it was time to collect my backpack from the Refugio and make the journey back to Refugio Paine Grande this time not to stay in the Refugio, but to camp in one of the already set up tents. Having received my sleeping bag, I unpacked my fleece sleeper bag liner which I had carried along and my self inflatable mat. The day had started nearly windstill and after I drifted off to sleep I was woken up at night time to the sound of battering wind and rain. The famous 100 km per hour winds of Patagonia had started and I prayed it would be dry again during the morning. Day 3 I woke up to the same strong wind, but otherwise a beautiful day. The day ahead would be one of the longest days and I was away by 9am. The countryside changed and I was walking through a recovering burned down forest. At that time the extent of the fire a few years ago was clearly visible and it was a pretty sad sight, but still stunningly enough with the high mountains rising to my left and the amazing azure blue lake to my right. After a few hours walk I reached one of the free camping sites which was also the starting point to climb up to Valley Frances. I had a quick bite to eat, dumped my heavy backpack and with my camera and water bottle, I set off through the forest up the hill. The wind was battering the trees above me and it was scary, but knowing that the trees withstand the winds all the time I moved along. To my left the views showed huge glaciers on mountains and the winds were so strong that the water of the waterfalls was pushed sideways and upways. During times the forest cleared and it was hard to stand without being blown over by the wind. Each time I was glad to be back in the forest which slowed down the wind. 2h later I had reached the view point, but knowing there was another one, I continued up the mountain. The path had stopped and a steep slope was ahead of me...I climbed for another half an hour until the views climbed above the trees. It was amazing and oh how much did I wished to walk further, but I knew that another 4-5h were still ahead so I returned. I had filled my water bottle a few times at the many streams, but I also cursed myself for not having brought any food ...I was starving! Finally 4.5 hours after setting off, I was back at my backpack and wolfed down some rather late lunch. The path continued climbing 2 small hills and I could feel the wind getting even stronger. The views were amazing and I stopped often to rest and take pictures. By the time the path reached the shore of the lake, it was time to put my feed into the 3 C cold water...I shrieked with the cold , but had 'New feet' for the first ten minutes after. After 10.5 hours I arrived at Refugio Los Cuernos. I was knackered and treated myself to a cold beer in the sunshine-Bliss! Day 4 Having eaten a lot of my foot (having started with the heaviest) my backpack was getting lighter and a relatively short 5h day lay ahead. I set off in the morning and the path crossed some pretty uneventful countryside. I enjoyed that every day the area was changing and did not get repetitive. The wind was still strong and after 3h walking time the path was climbing again and a amazing valley opened up to me. In the distance I could see my next Refugio and it was nice to meet people I had met during the last few days throughout the day. Refugio Torre central is the last one before the famous Torres and even though I had thought to climb up to the Torres during the same day, the previous day had left me tired and I was happy to chill out and watch the Gauchos delivering food with their horses. Day 5 Everyone will recommend to get up before sunrise at 3am and walk to the Towers which was supposed to be a 2h walk for sunrise at 5am. I am not a morning person and getting up at 3 am to walk up a mountain, is the last thing which I will call an enjoyable activity. So regardless of the pity stares I got when I announced I will walk up when I wake up (I did not care) I went to bed at 22:00h and slept until 8am, waking up to glorious sunshine. The people who had looked down to me and set off at 3am were back with dire faces. They had set off in torrential rain, mixed with snow and thick clouds had prevented any view or imaged of a sunrise...the early bird , not always gets the worm! With a smirk in my face I set off at 9am (this time taking food with me) and made my way up the hill. The main part is through a forest and only towards the end opens up to a huge steep boulder field. Signs warn you to follow the path and even though you want to ignore them and take the seemingly easier routes, they make sense, as otherwise you would be on a even steeper slope right down the glacier lake. I arrived in glorious sunshine 1.15h after setting off , the Torres in front of me and only another two people in sight. They soon left and I was alone with magnificent views all to myself. The views were stunning and even though I had enjoyed my solitude, I was glad to see some people appearing about half an hour later...after all I had wanted some photos. I managed to stay up for 1.5h and afterwards the cold drove me back down and on my way towards the last Refugio. Day 6 The last Refugio had been spacious which was just as well, as I had to wait until 2 pm to catch the bus back to Puerto Natales. review_text_preprocessed: Patagonia and Torres del Paine was a life long dream and living in Scotland meant that it was no easy place to get to. The cheapest flights I could find was a trip from Glasgow to New York, New York to Houston/Texas, Houston to Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires to Santiago/Chile, Santiago Chile to Punta Arenas/Chile. The total flight time was 27.5h. Punta Arenas is a town next to the Strait of Malagan and I loved the colourful wooden houses and the friendly people, who I met when I explored the city.I only stayed for a day, as the Trek I had planned, in the famous Torres del Paine National Park, was still a 5h bus journey away. The hostel had helped me to book a bus ticket to Puerto Natales (closest town to the park) and after a 3h bus journey I was finally at my destination. In the town most of the Hostels and many shops rent out all sorts of equipment and in a number of outdoor stores you can buy what ever you need. I had taken most gear with me from home and to rent a pair of walking poles for 6 days set me back 10 Pounds (not bad). The Erratic Rock Hostel in Punta Arenas arranged a daily information talk in the Base Camp Pub next door and useful information incl. were you should not drink water from the streams were given out over a relaxing cup of tea, coffee or a pint. Camping or Refugios The Trek itself can be done via a Tour Company (the easiest) or by organising everything yourself. I opted for the latter as it is the most cost effective way. The first question you should ask yourself, is if you want to camp or stay in basic accommodation (Refugios). If you want to camp you can either carry all your camping gear, or rent it is the park. Please be aware that wild camping is strictly forbidden, as well as making a fire. You will have to camp in the designated camping areas (between free and 10 Pounds a night) and most have toilets, bathrooms with showers and kitchen areas. Prepared food can be bought in the Refugios (around 25 Pounds for Breakfast, Lunch and dinner) or you buy your food before hand and carry it. If you want to stay in the Refugios you will have to book ahead of time. I booked 4 months in advance and one place was already booked out! So do it at least half a year in advance, if you want to have a warm comfortable bed. Rooms usually have 8 beds and were a lot better than I had imagined. The W, O or Q Trek The 2 main treks people do are the W or O Trek. Simply called W and O by the shape you walk it. The O trek requires you to carry your own tent and camping equipment , as a few places do not have Refugios and only designated camping areas with basic toilets. The W covers the most stunning parts of the walk and the W allows you to choose Refugios or campsites. I opted for the W Trek starting from Lago Grey (anticlockwise) and finish at the famous Torres. The Trek Day 1 Having stayed the day and night in Pueto Natales, I had managed to book the bus to the park, buy enough food to last me for 6 days and pack my backpack. Having paid my entrance fee, together with lots of other people, everyone had to watch a information programme and were reminded that causing a fire can result in a 20 year prison sentence. Harsh, but a few years ago a backpacker caused a wildfire which burned down a huge area of the park, so it made sense. Afterwards everyone was moved back to the bus for another hours travel to the Catamaran to cross Pehoé Lake. The bus arrived with an hour to spare and apart from waiting around, I made the short walk to Salto Grande an impressive waterfall. Having spend far too much time at the fall I nearly missed the boat - ups. Safely on board the trip over the lake was stunning. Ahead the 'Horns' were poking out of the clouds and the fact I was finally in Patagonia sank in. Soon the 45min journey came to an end and I stood in front of Refugio Paine Grande were the walk started and I would return to on day 2. I set off and soon the full weight of my 16 kilo backpack started to show. I was glad for my walking poles, but my hips and legs were struggling with the unfamiliar weight. The path lead up a slight slope through the burned down country side (due to the huge fire caused by the backpacker) and apart from the burned down trees, the countryside reminded me strongly about Scotland. 2 hours into the walk a lake came into view and on were 'Icebergs'. Wow Wow Wow! I stood there for a good ten minutes amazed and excited...I had not expected that. The path lead up a small hill and from the top the edge of Glacier Grey could be seen. A glacier ending in a lake must be one of the most impressive sights on earth and the big grin on my face stayed until I reached the lovely Refugio Grey. The rooms were clean and warm with amazing comfortable beds. I dumped my backpack and headed into the shower, had some food and chatted to a few other walkers I had met during the walk. The days in December are long up to 18h of sunlight in winter time and together with one of my friends, I went for a walk down to the lake edge. On the water a big Iceberg could be seen not far away and along the shore were hundreds of broken off peaces of ice which were floating in the ice cold water. So 'cool' Day 2 Due to the fact that only a short 4h day lay ahead of me, I had decided to take a 3h kayaking trip on Lago Grey. The cost of the trip included full equipment and a short lesson of how to kayak. I was joined up with another unexperienced woman in one kayak, but we managed fine and had a marvellous time kayaking around the glacier. We were so lucky when right in front of us (yet in save distance) 2 huge peaces of the ice broke off and crashed into the water. The sound of it I will never forget and the short walking trip right to the edge close the most compacted ice which appears dark blue was definitely one of the highlights of the trip. After the kayaking trip it was time to collect my backpack from the Refugio and make the journey back to Refugio Paine Grande this time not to stay in the Refugio, but to camp in one of the already set up tents. Having received my sleeping bag, I unpacked my fleece sleeper bag liner which I had carried along and my self inflatable mat. The day had started nearly windstill and after I drifted off to sleep I was woken up at night time to the sound of battering wind and rain. The famous 100 km per hour winds of Patagonia had started and I prayed it would be dry again during the morning. Day 3 I woke up to the same strong wind, but otherwise a beautiful day. The day ahead would be one of the longest days and I was away by 9am. The countryside changed and I was walking through a recovering burned down forest. At that time the extent of the fire a few years ago was clearly visible and it was a pretty sad sight, but still stunningly enough with the high mountains rising to my left and the amazing azure blue lake to my right. After a few hours walk I reached one of the free camping sites which was also the starting point to climb up to Valley Frances. I had a quick bite to eat, dumped my heavy backpack and with my camera and water bottle, I set off through the forest up the hill. The wind was battering the trees above me and it was scary, but knowing that the trees withstand the winds all the time I moved along. To my left the views showed huge glaciers on mountains and the winds were so strong that the water of the waterfalls was pushed sideways and upways. During times the forest cleared and it was hard to stand without being blown over by the wind. Each time I was glad to be back in the forest which slowed down the wind. 2h later I had reached the view point, but knowing there was another one, I continued up the mountain. The path had stopped and a steep slope was ahead of me...I climbed for another half an hour until the views climbed above the trees. It was amazing and oh how much did I wished to walk further, but I knew that another 4-5h were still ahead so I returned. review_text: THE HORSE TRIP One trip takes you up to a rock with spectacular views on lake Sofia. Of course this is a trip that's done many times. But still, it feels very unique. Eagles and condors were flying above, a sign of luck. The forest we passed was mysterious. The team of workers and volunteers is very welcoming and passionated in what they are doing. Cristian, the man who guided, was very attentive. We had a nice cup of fresh coffee on the top. I had the luck to go on my own. I met a group of 6 beginners. Also for them, it was great and doable. The other trip is to beautiful lake Sofia with more galloping and trotting. Practically: Before the horse trip you get leather legprotections and a quality protection hat. Take a vest agaist the rain (no plastic poncho as horses get afraid of this) and a windstopper. Gloves might be handy. THE COTTAGE Stay at least one night! The cottage is just perfect. Rustic and decorated with style and quality materials, with a stove on wood, 2 clean bathrooms with hot showers, a great mattress and spectacular views from the living room and the 2 bedrooms (dorms of 7or8 people). The horses are gathered around the house before taking off for a trip. That's quiet a welcome in the morning. It's a very good price-quality deal. There's no wifi nor phone connection. It's a perfect retreat place. If there's something urgent the team will help you. I wanted to cancel a hotel reservation - as I decided to stay longer at PingoSalvaje - and Paula took care of the phone call. You can camp in a beautiful camping but be prepared for the weather conditions. Practically: Take all the food and drinks with you. As you are in the middle of nature, there's no supermarket whatsoever around. There's a fridge in the cottage and you can cook on a simple electric stove. Don't envision making complicated meals. There's one pan, cutlery and plates. You can also order an asado (for lunch or dinner). In the cottage there are quality sleeping bags you can use. HOW TO GET THERE Send a email with your request and the asked details on the website (name, nationality, length -to know which horse they have to saddle for you- etc). If you have no own car, there's no way to get there by public transport, which makes it also such a special and safe place as there's no one. If you want a pick up from Puerto Natales, mention the time and the location.

review_text: This winery is a gem! We had booked a tour in advance through our tour guide and were thrilled when we arrived! The experience was VIP! Francisco met us and immediately poured us a glass of Sauvignon Blanc and showed us the tasting room, then the four of us walked down into the vineyards. Amazing to be drinking wine while standing next to the grapes still growing on the vines! He told us about the history of the vineyard and also showed us where they had recently grafted some new vines. Fascinating! When we headed back inside, he poured us some wine directly out of the fermenting tanks so we could taste the wine as its current stage. Then we headed into the cellar to view the barrels, and then up to the third floor to sit at a beautiful glass table while we drank more of their delicious wine while eating cheese, bread and local olive oil. The whole tour was fantastic and although it was pricer than the other wineries we visited, it was totally worth it! It was an amazing experience and I highly recommend it!

review_text: Our visit to Cousiño Macul was beyond excellent. We had originally opted for the traditional tour but changed to the premium once there, and were very glad we did (see below). The traditional tour was with a wonderful guide (Janice) who knew everything about the winery and its long history and was happy to spend quite a bit of extra time talking about Chilean food and traditions. We were lucky to be in a small group (3) so there was plenty of time to talk! Once the traditional tour was over, my wife and I were in for the great treat of tasting 3 of Cousiño Macul's premium wines: two from their "Finis Terrae" line (the first was an incredible white wine made from a blend of Chardonnay, Riesling and Viogner, the other a striking red blend), the third bottle was from their a collection simply called "W" an amazing Cabernet Sauvignon. What made this part of the tour so rewarding was our "guide" through the tasting, Frederico (I'm sorry of I got the name wrong, it might have been Federico). Frederico knew everything there was to know about the wines, the grapes, labor and love that had gone into making them. he helped us puzzle our way through the rich tastes of these wines intelligently and with a subtle sense of humor and pride in Chile's wines that left a deep impression on us. As a trained sommelier and aspiring oenologist, we could not have asked for a better guide. Thank you to Janice, Frederico and Cousiño Macul for one of the most memorable experiences during our one-month stay in Santiago. On the practical side, if you are visiting in February go for the early tour (10am) before the afternoon heat sets in! Review of: Premium Wine Tour in Viña Cousiño Macul Spanish official

review_text: Might be a brief, useful diversion for the kids on a rainy day ... but only if they're fluent in Spanish, because there are no English descriptions at all. Even then, I'm not sure I would bother. I went because the collection purportedly includes some original Rongorongo tablets from Easter Island. (Only a few authentic ones survive, and none on the island itself.) But the museum's entire Easter Island display consists of a few wood carvings, one bird petroglyph, and a small, eroded moai. When I asked the woman behind the counter if any authentic tablets are in fact in their collection, she had no idea what I was talking about. When I asked if I could speak to someone who might have the answer, she said "no". There is a blue whale skeleton in the main room, for some reason, and upstairs, a replica of an Andes sacrificial mummy (again, they claim to have the original but do not display it), a few dioramas, and that's it. Admission is free. My advice: find somewhere else to amuse the kids on a rainy day. Thank you for your comments. We have audioguides in english that you can request in our access hall. We have original rongorongo tablets, but they are in storage in our anthropology area. They are part of the exhibition during the 1980's. Beforte the 2010 earthquake we had a entire Easter Island room in the second floor, but we had to close it, because of the damage that the building suffered. We have a 3D version of the original tablets, which you can check here: https://sketchfab.com/MNHNcl/collections/rapa-nui The whale skeleton that's in our main hall is a Sei Whale, is the symbol of our museum: http://www.mnhn.gob.cl/sitio/Contenido/Colecciones-digitales/5028:Ballena-del-MNHN-oculta-un-siglo-su-identidad (in spanish). We have a replica of the El Plomo Hill mummy in the exhibition of our first floor. The original is stored in an special chamber in the anthropology area. Here's a brochure in english with more information: https://issuu.com/mnhn_cl/docs/folleto_nino_cerro_el_plomo_ingles_ If you need further assistance or have more questions you can reach us at comunicaciones@mnhn.cl

review_text: Its the only way to explore the southern fjords in Chile and they make the most money out of it, as they know it. I had a room with 2 bunk beds but was happy that i did not have to share it with another person as it is really small and has nearly no space if you are travelling with bigger luggage. The breakfast, lunch and dinner are really basic which i normally don't mind but if i am paying 550 US$ i expect a bit more. It was presented so loveless, the soups without taste and just instant Nescafe for breakfast. Take some additional snacks and drinks on board if you are going for the trip because you cannot buy anything apart from oreos on board. Apart from things mentioned above, i want to say thank you Percy for your very interesting lectures which you have done with so much enthusiasm and passion for what you are doing. Thanks a lot.

review_text: This was our 4th trip to Chile for summer skiing and the best one yet! We had the good fortune to find Santiago Adventures 3 years ago, and have relied on them for our annual trips ever since. Our grasp of the Spanish language is minimal at best (but working on it) so we really needed some guidance/help planning our trips. They took our vague list of "things we wanted to do & see" and formulated a wonderful adventure for us. Brian's suggestions of Powder Lodge and the wine tasting after skiing on Friday were perfect. Our billingual driver Manuel was charming & extremely knowledgeable-he could help translate as well as give background on the different varieties, vineyards, and various sights on the way up and down from Farrellones. I didn't even fall asleep on the drive (I usually can't help it). Even though we have never met, I feel like Brian knows us and anticipates our every want/need. We look forward to many more ski trips with Santiago adventures at the helm.

review_text: I forgot our guide's name (tour on 28-Dec). We took this tour on our first day of arrival in Santiago . . . it was a nice overview, and the guide was very good in making sure his commentary was provided in both Spanish and English. He was friendly. However as we realized a few days later, the tour wasn't as complete as was suggested in the promotional material. Perhaps the tour is a bit more variable in content...? But there were some inconsistencies with what is noted as 'included' in the material that weren't quite so. For example: we may have 'seen' Santa Lucia from the top of San Cristobal, but we certainly did not visit it on this tour. The material suggests that the entry/admission to Cerro San Cristobal was included in the tour fee. To get to the statue/hilltop, you have to take a funicular which involves a fee that was NOT included in the tour. Further --- our guide stayed back at the waiting area while we all went to buy a ticket where we then found out there are a number of ticket options (all in Spanish). If this is your experience, you want only the ticket that takes you to the top; you don't want the zoo or the tram that goes to the other side; there is no time (on this tour) to do those things. So ask around (or ask the ticket-sales person) which ticket. All in all, this an ok tour. If nothing else, this was a nice diversion for our first day to help us stay awake after a very long travel experience. Review of: Half-Day Small-Group Panoramic Santiago Tour Thank you for sharing your experience with us! We're deeply regretful over the inconveniences, and we'll work hard so this doesn't happen again. We'll work hard to be better in the future. MTO Tour Team

review_text: We returned to Punta Pirulil and Muelle de las Ánimas, just to find that if you are not paying a travel agent, or are willing to spend your day guessing how to enter, it is almost impossible to access the famous attraction, even on a Saturday. We got as close as you can get to the entrance to the Muelle, and the parking lot was closed, but no signs saying anything, only locked. Since there was no one around we parked on the side of the road and starting walking. After probably 1.5 km, on a beautiful but muddy road through the hills, we got to a locked fence with several signs. One of them, that was nailed, read “closed, we will we back tomorrow at 09.00” (suspicious, since it was nailed), another one read “no trespassing” and the third one read “1.500 entrance fee”. No signs, whatsoever on how to enter the place. So we did what we shouldn´t have done, and make an extra effort jumping the fence. Since there were no signs anywhere on how to enter or saying that the place was closed, we decided to continue with our trip. Once we continued our walk we met a guide that explained us how to enter legally. What you have to do is return to the parking lot and drive back about 3 km to a house were they have the key, and pay there. The place is beautiful, and the whole “bridge” or “quay/dock” idea is good, but I think it is insane that there are no signs anywhere saying that you need a key, or where the key is, and that after a couple of km. of walk you find a locked gate with no signs indicating how to enter the place. And after walking to the car, and driving to get the key, THEY CHARGE YOU! The place is beautiful, AMAZING, and the walk is nice, but the “service” is terrible, they should worry about the tourists that are visiting them and have more indications and signs somewhere. By the way, if you want to go, the key is found in the group of houses on the right of the road, just before the bridge by the beach. And if the weather isn´t blue skies, be sure to bring a rain jacket with you, it gets windy and wet!

review_text: Las Loberias Hotel, Laguna San Rafael promenade. Good intentions and a sum of bad decisions. We began the journey with great enthusiasm at 8 in the morning, with an unstable day, clouds, rain and some clear sunshine. We were 204 anxious and expectant passengers. After 4 hours of navigation at 24 nautical miles per hour, we sighted the immense block of ice. The first group, which boarded one of the boats to get closer to the eternal ice, set sail with quite a few waves. The second group suffered the same fate. I was part of the third group, until then the captain had expressed the best intentions, so that everyone could get as close as possible to the snowdrift. But that was the beginning of bad decisions. Only 7 tourists managed to get on. Me with my husband and two children. And next to us were two 11-year-old boys and the older brother. The waves and wind caused the boat to move away from the catamaran, making it impossible for the rest of the participants in group 3 to get on. But, beneath the good intentions of having the entire group 3 board the boat, came the second bad decision. The captain approached the shore seeking shelter from the wind and ran aground. There came the third bad decision, with us in the boat, maneuvers began to try to hit the boat and in this way help it run aground. This action was repeated three times, denoting a serious lack of protocol, placing the passengers, in this case us, in the middle of a very dangerous and primitive maneuver. This lasted until my husband asked to be taken off the boat, so as not to risk our safety. We were able to re-embark on the Catamaran and after many efforts, acceleration, and also the supreme self of the tide, the boat ran aground. And after 15 minutes, we, group 3, were asked to return to the first floor with the life jackets to try again. The waves were still huge. Finally, sanity prevailed, and it was decided not to continue with the boat trips and begin the return to Puerto Chacabuco. But the ship had suffered some damage from the grounding, the speed was decreasing, the lights went out, the electrical system stopped working and with it the bathrooms. Tempers also began to fray. In search of answers within the passengers, the captain was able to come down to give an explanation of the situation after three hours of uncertainty and murmurs. The trip continued at very low speed, increasing the return trip by three additional hours, arriving at 00:30 hrs, completely dark. In my opinion, it is necessary to review the security protocols. If from the first minute it had been decided not to lower the boats, a chain of bad decisions would have been avoided, which ended with a disastrous experience.

I highly, highly recommend it.

review_text: We booked a total of three days with Chilean wine lovers and went to 8 wineries across three days: Our approach was not to go to Chile to buy 6 dollar wines. Rather it was to get wines to add to our cellar at great prices that we can drink years down the road. Although we tasted a few $6-10 wines that were lovely too. My favorite wineries for wine: 1. Casa Del Bosque - CWL takes you here for a reason. Great estate wines and great prices. 2. RE: blended wines, different techniques and the results are fantastic. Not cheap wines but completely unique tastes. Well worth it. 3. Emiliana: beautiful vineyard and lovely affordable wines for under 20 that drink like 40 plus dollar wines from Napa or France. 4. Errazuriz: Award winning and steeped in history for a reason. Again we bought a few lovely wines. I'm not suggesting the other 4 we went to weren't good but these were the highlights for me and my husband. Prettiest Vineyard, just go for the beauty: 1. Casa Del Esteban - breathtakingly lovely. Surpised by: 1. How many wineries have very good Sauvignon blanc.... I'm not a white wine drinker. But loves these. Easy to drink and great as an Apertif: House of Morande Sauvignon blanc, and Casas Del Bosque Sauvignon Blanc. Chilean Wine Lovers: Gonazalo is simply the best. Professional, knowledgeable, an ambassador of all things Chilean. We loved everyday with him. We also met Mauricio on our last day. He personally organized our meals at the wineries as we needed to accommodate a vegetarian. Can't thank them enough for the loveliest trip! You will not go wrong by booking with Chilean Wine Lovers.

review_text: I never doubted that I would go up this hill to admire the views, so the length of the queue would not have deterred me. But travelling up and back via the funicular railway meant that I was in a very slow queue (as the funicular is slow) going up, and a slightly faster queue coming down. It may be wise to get there very early to avoid this, especially if you have children with you. The funicular ticket can be combined with a cable car (ropeway, called teleferico) which is a good idea. The newish cable car gives some good views and is an easy way to traverse part of the large hill. Views from the top would be good on a good day, but it was a bit hazy on the day that I went, so my advice is to choose the day carefully if you have a choice. There's not really a lot to see at the top except for the view, although a visit to the statue of the virgin and the prayer area, in readiness for Pope Francis' visit in January 2018, is easy to do and worth the trouble. In all, a bit disappointing, and I preferred Cerro Santa Lucia.

review_text: These are the caverns close to the volcano, and they have fully reopened. There’s a big cafe with an expansive view but a very limited menu ... machine coffee and buns, basically. Our guide was young and enthusiastic, but with no English. I was part of a tour group, and our tour guide spoke Spanish, while my sister is also fluent and translated for us all. There’s a small information/interpretive centre, and from there you walk over to the caves to collect your hard hat. The descent to the caves is uneven but relatively easy. I was okay for the first 15 minutes or so, but then there was a steep ladder-style descent and, being 60, I bunked out at that point. More intrepid travellers carried on and emerged alive, but did say it was “more of the same”. I think you’ll get more from the visit if you speak Spanish and are really interested in lava tubes! Near the entrance is a beaten-up truck largely encased in lava ... probably the most memorable thing there ... it was brought down the road by a Lahar and dumped there, much to the delight of our tourists cameras.

review_text: I went to the Viña Undurraga half day winery tour, although we only spent about 90 minutes at the vineyard, we spent much more time in buses. The shuttle was 15 minutes late to pick me up from the time I was instructed to wait in my hotel lobby. We were transported to the main mall and then I was told to stay on the bus, while everyone else got off and went to other tour buses. We waited another 20 minutes or so, and then finally people started piling in. We left for the valley and the "tour" was presented in both Spanish and English. There were only two English speakers on the tour, so it felt awkward at times to be spoken to over the bus' PA system when we were both sitting just a few feet away. We arrived at the winery. There was some confusion for the first 15-20 minutes as we milled about and tried to figure out what we were supposed to do. The gift shop was small and didn't have many items for sale. Finally, I found the tour guide who said he'd give us a sticker to wear so we could participate in the tour. He disappeared and I found him many minutes later. Finally the tour started. The whole process upon arrival seemed confusing, but maybe it just wasn't clarified in English. The English speaking tour was much smaller, even with some other tour buses joining us. It was an okay tour and the guide spoke good English and was fairly knowledgeable about winemaking and the vineyard itself. At times we seemed to compete with the Spanish speaking tour and it was difficult to hear and navigate through certain areas as they were coming or we were going. The tasting was fine - we had a Sav Blanc, Cab, Carmenere, and some sweet blend that she never mentioned the name. The reds were my favorite, and while we got to keep our wine glass that had the vineyard's name on it, I was a bit put off that we were not able to get another (even small) pour of our favorite. It seemed very different than any other winery tour I'd been on. Also, it was clear that the majority of the group were not to familiar with wine or wine tasting, so it surprised me that the guide didn't give tips on tasting, beyond listing off some of the basic smells and tastes you may experience with each wine. We were given bad crackers in between the reds. And that was it for the tour. The gift shop was small, and they didn't seem prepared to help ship or sell wine. I asked a few questions about purchasing wine in hopes of figuring out what would be more efficient. I was basically told, it was twice the price plus shipping to get the wine shipped through an importer and there was no question or offer to sell me any at the store to take with me. I simply got a warning that I couldn't take more than two bottles with me and that was it. I didn't want a hard sell of wine, but couldn't believe they were not more interesting in selling me anything. Next time, I think I'd pay a little extra to do a smaller or private tour that could include more than one vineyard. The hassle with the buses and the just okay tour was not enough for me to want to recommend this to someone. TIP: Purchase your ticket online and save 10%, at least that is the current deal I saw after I booked through my hotel concierge. We appreciate your comment dear traveler, it is very important for us to know about your experience.

review_text: This site is close to San Pedro de Atacama so is often one of the first locations visited on a trip to that area. It is usually coupled with a sunset view. The valley is rather rough with interesting desert views and some very large sand dunes. One of the more interesting locations is an old salt mine with great views of the surrounding valley. However, be advised that to reach it you need to climb through sand from a huge sand dune and up a fairly steep trail. This might be better left to a second or third day to allow acclimation to the high altitude. Following the trip to the valle, we headed to a high point to watch the sunset. It was not too exciting as the sky was perfectly clear without the clouds that make sunsets so beautiful. However, we had a huge full moon to watch on our trip back to our hotel.

review_text: FotoRuta is a very original way to experience Santiago, and especially one of its most picturesque parts - Barrio Lastarria. It does not matter if you have lived in Santiago for years, or you just arrived for a short visit - this tour is definitiely worth taking. The first thing to mention is the fact that this is not an ordinary tour. You do not follow a guide, or learn something new about Santago's history. What you learn, however, is to open your eyes to everyday details you would have missed otherwise. You learn to capture an image of a little girl playing with her parents, or of a lazy dog sleeping the summer heat off. You are welcome and even encouraged to chat with locals and politely ask them to take photos of them. And afterwards, everybody shows their photographs and gets feedback and profesional advice while enjoying a glass of wine... So, what's not to like? This tour is focused on photograpy and every amateur or professional photographer should definitely take it as it will improve their skill. Maybe the best thing of this tour is the way it changes, forever, the way you look at the world around you.

review_text: We drove out to see the spectacular huge rock formations known as "the Monks". There are more than one places nearby where one can enjoy the views of the desert, lakes and fauna. Our guide took us to a vantage point overlooking this beautiful lake, and then produced a very tasty sit-down lunch. We were able to watch very large flocks of flamingos wading in the water just below us - they had mated only a week before, but not yet commenced nest building. The site also provided a spectacular view of the surrounding volcanos. This is one of our favourite places in the Atacama.

review_text: We were picked up promptly by Sebastian from our hotel. The vehicle was clean and comfortable and water was waiting for us. Sebastian has the most excellent English and coped well with my hearing problem. He was thoughtful, informative and flexible as well as funny and charming. We felt safe as he was an excellent driver. Sebastian recognised that seeing llamas by the side of the road was amazing for us and parked close, but not too close so I could take lots of photos. We enjoyed his knowledge of the wildlife and vegetation. He explained that we couldn’t visit the village of Rio Grande because of a dangerous road after recent heavy rain but made up for this by showing us some ancient carvings and a wonderful viewpoint instead. The Rainbow Valley visit was memorable. The colours are every bit as wonderful as the adverts show and Sebastian explained about how they were formed. We went later in the afternoon and it was very quiet. We only met two people during our walk. What impressed me was that Sebastian understood me when I said I liked to feel dwarfed by nature and drove us a little further into the valley to some amazing rock passages. We finished at Death Valley to watch the sunset. A great spot as the views were amazing. Sebastian was an excellent host and we enjoyed the wine and goodies he’d brought with him. A wonderful day and a wonderful guide. Many thanks Sebastian. Jill and Brian Shield

We had a blast on the tour -- the guides were capable in English and Spanish and provided nice bikes and helmets that were safe and well-cared-for. The day trip was a great bargain -- we rode through two wineries and sampled wines out of the vat at each, learned a great deal about the region's Maipo Valley wine industry, and our small group had hors d'oeuvres outside and then a long lunch with plenty of wine. The tour was entirely on flat terrain so it's alright for everyone who might want to participate. It was one of the top 3 things I did while in Chile -- highly recommend the bike and wine tour.

review_text: I like to see at least a bit of the local scenery/culture on a business trip as otherwise all you experience is the airplane/hotel/meeting which pretty much is the same thing anywhere you go in the world. On this last trip I was in Santiago with my wife and we took a foodyChile tour. We asked for a trip out to the coast rather than Santiago itself, which foodyChile set up as a day excursion to Valparaiso via the Casablanca valley. Our Casablanca tour included a visit to the Bodega Re winery, an artisan producer highly regarded in wine circles and using historic production methods. And with some rather good wines which we tasted. Then on to Valpo for food and to explore the old town. Valpo is very hilly, so we were pleased that there were funicular railways to get us to the top before walking mostly downhill… there are extensive murals in the old town and the tour was focused on those, more wine, and seafood. However, I found the buildings in the old town fascinating in themselves – I’m from Canada and Valpo old town reminded me a bit of St John’s. Just a lovely afternoon walking around before winding up at the harbour to experience some local craft ale. The guides were both knowledgeable and organized. We were collected after breakfast by our guide and returned back to the hotel by early evening – indeed a full day, and just what we needed as a zero-effort tour to add on to our business trip. Most enjoyable and excellent value for money !! Thank you for taking the time to leave us such a nice review. We're glad you could find a little time to mix some pleasure in with your business and happy we could help. We love Valpo and we're glad you found it as interesting as we do. We hope to see you back down this way again. All the best!

review_text: We travelled south to north, from Puerto Natales to Puerto Montt. You know that picture on their web page that shows people looking at the glacier? It's a fantasy, we never saw a glacier - maybe we passed it in the night and you only see it if you travel north to south. Actually there was really not much to see at all, there was a rumour someone spotted a dolphin but not confirmed. If you do this trip once a week for 10 years, you'll probably see some good stuff. The cabins weren't bad - we had the AAA with window and private bathroom - but otherwise limited places to hang out. They had a 'reading room' which was not heated and ridiculously cold, so the only place to sit was the dining room, and only two tables there had a view, so all the passengers had to fight over them. The also had a theatre/cinema, but they only seemed to play football matches in Spanish for the crew to watch. They said they would show movies for the passengers, but the only time they did was when I hunted down the appropriate person and hounded him into putting a movie on. (and the english speaking staff really did have to be hunted down - they were nowhere to be found most of the time and got very annoyed if you went into their dining room to ask for something). There is no alcohol on board and no music, so I don't understand how they can show pictures of people partying and having fun. The shop/bar seems only to open a couple of hours in the evening and sells bugger all. They had a game of bingo on the last night which was the only form of entertainment. Pathetic really. The food was adequate. The best thing was the wildlife talks for about an hour each day. Fascinating to hear about all the things we might have seen but didn't. The worst thing was the four truckloads of cattle who we watched endure five nights crammed in together in the wind and the rain, while the smell worsened to the point you didn't even want to venture out on to the deck. All in all we were frankly bored witless - take a good book. Take the Navimag if you have plenty of money and time to waste and don't care about comfort, service or food!

review_text: It's beautiful, really is. But there's too many people - be great if they restricted the numbers somehow. We did the "O" over 9 days - worth doing. Book asap, especially if you want to stay at Torres camp to make it up for sunrise. Remember you can only go anti-clockwise on the back end - the booking system doesn't manage this. The Refugios are ridiculously over priced - disgusting that the parks all such exorbitant prices. Zero ethics there. Experts - ignore this just know that there are mice at the campsites so hang your food. Once you get on the back leg it's less busy as they limit the trail to 80 people starting per day. Ignore any other info about route times and distances as they're all wrong and very over stated. Intermediates - Its a decent hike. If you've vaguely fit and know what you're doing you will definitely be under the times stated. When going over the pass there's no need to start at 7am in the morning with head torches even if you're going to Grey - it's a 7 hour hike from Perros to Grey!! (11hrs guideline is there for the beginners). No specific need to stay at Paso however if you have good weather it's a nice small camp. Going from Italiano to Torres is more than possible to avoid the full board refugios. Beginners - stick to the hotels at the bottom, do everyone a favor! There's too many of your types washing dishes in the river, making noise, being inconsiderate and generally not being very environmentally friendly.

review_text: We had an unforgettable stargazing tour with Jorge. The communication in advance was uncomplicated and the pickup on the day of the tour as agreed. Finally, on Jorge's private property, we first got an astronomy class in which Jorge explained the basics of astronomy in a captivating way. This was followed by a break with delicious food and drinks from an impressive buffet prepared by his wife. Eventually, we were able to observe numerous objects ourselves through the various telescopes, which was the highlight of the tour. Jorge shone with his extensive knowledge of the night sky and was able to answer every question without any problems. Finally, Jorge took group as well as individual photos of us in front of the Milky Way, which turned out really great. All in all, the tour was definitely worth the money. Especially positive is that the tour was scheduled for about three hours, but actually lasted about five hours.

With guide Jose Miguel from Huella Andina Expediciones we drove as far as we could with the 4WD to the base. We crossed some private properties. This area is heavely covered with small stones from the explosion. Some of the trees are getting new leaves and smaller shrubs are pushing through the ashes. The very interesting aspect of the walk is the forest which is in process of recuperation after the volcano explosion. New leaves are coming from the lower stem sections, while the tops of the trees have been stripped bare by the falling gravel. Higher up, stones the size of tennis balls were found. Sitting above the top line of vegetation a Condor came very close (20 m ?) to have look, but we did not have time to grab our camera.

review_text: On 22/08/2024 I took the horse ride in the Yerba Loca park, which was the best tour of the 6 days I was present in Santiago. Although I have hired other agencies to do popular tours such as ski day, portillo, vineyards, etc, I have to admit that Indo Pro Chile stands out with this ecological nature tour. We finished the tour with a barbecue/picnic inside the park, with wine, snacks, Brazilian-style barbecue, Chilean-style choripan and the excellent service of our Chilean Guide Juan, who did everything possible to make our tour memorable from start to finish. It is worth noting that the Guide Juan has specific certifications and qualifications in the area of tourism, so the presence of professionals like him end up refining the quality of the tour, from the pick up in the accommodation to the return to the metropolitan region of Santiago. If I had more time in Chile, I would ⁇ have asked Indo Pro Chile to assign me to the riding of the Bosque Ciprestes, which has a different footprint from the Yerba Loca ride. Strangely, few people know this type of tour in Chile, even when showing the photos and videos of my tour to other tourists, many were surprised that they were not aware of these possibilities. Making an ecological tour, as close to Santiago, as in the case of Yerba Loca, is a "no brainer" for any vacationer.

review_text: We had an incredible half-day tour of Santiago that was the perfect blend of culture, history, and stunning sights! Our guide, Leonardo, was fantastic—friendly and passionate about taking us to view this vibrant city. The only thing we wish is that he could know more about the history of the city, country, and the places we go as well as answer the questions we ask about the trees and flowers we saw on our way to each place. The tour started with a visit to the Cerro San Cristóbal, which offered breathtaking panoramic views of the city and the Andes mountains—absolutely a must-see! Another stop that was astonishing was the historic Plaza de Armas, where we learned about Santiago’s colonial past and its transformation into a modern metropolis. We also explored the charming neighborhoods of Las Condes and Vitacura, which were full of colorful street art, quaint shops, and local cafes. The guide made sure to point out hidden gems and gave us tips for places to revisit on our own. The pace of the tour was just right, and the transportation was comfortable and punctual. This half-day experience was ideal for getting a great overview of Santiago without feeling rushed. The most important thing is that the guide made us feel very safe to stay in Santiago, although we heard about the issue happening there. I highly recommend this tour to anyone visiting Santiago—it’s a wonderful way to experience the city’s highlights in a short time. Perfect for history buffs, culture enthusiasts, or anyone who loves great views and good company! Review of: City tour by Santiago of Chile -A beautiful experience - Half day

review_text: Museo de Arte Precolumbino (open Tuesday-Sunday 10:00 to 18:00) has a good collection, which is nicely displayed, with signs written in excellent English. It is not the best museum in Chile, however. That would be Museo Colchagua in Santa Cruz 180 km. SW of Santiago. It is worth the trip if combined with a winery visit or two. Why is such a great museum in such a small place (Santa Cruz has a population of ~33,000)? Santa Cruz is the home of wealthy businessman Carlos Cardoen (among other things the creator of the cluster bomb). The museum is basically his collection and is run by his foundation. By the way, there is still an international arrest warrant out for him for arms sales to Iraq during Saddam Hussein's rule.

review_text: The guides were great and kept a good pace in order to make it to the top in time. I got a cramp in my leg on the way up and I had two guides sit down with me to massage the camp out. Then they took me up at a slightly slower pace from the rest of the group to make sure I was ok. This company gave us face masks when at the top due to the sulphur. I have asthma and found it hard to breathe at the mouth of the volcano. The masks helped a lot! Not all tour companies provide this so its worth checking before committing to the tour. Also the rest of the gear they provided was in pretty good condition. Some companies we checked out had ripped bags, some provided no jackets or trousers. I would say that our lunch break could have been longer. But I understand we were against the clock to make it up in time. But we literally got 15-20 minutes sitting on snow/ice on the side of the mountain to eat our sandwiches whilst having our crampons tied to our boots by the guides. The other rest stops were 5 minute breathers whilst standing up. It was still great and I loved it the whole day. This company made sure safety was the top priority which made them 5/5.

review_text: Valparaiso is a spectacular city holding on to the mountainside for dear life. One of the most important ports of South America at a time, it remains an important port for Chile today. The port, and the narrow flatland that surrounds it, are the site of the historical center, including Plaza Sotomayor and the Monument to the Heroes of Iquique, and important historical point in Chilean history. From there, you are on the ascent. The rest of the city was built at a 45 degree angle and it is a steep climb. Take a car or one of the old lifts the residents use to get around. The homes and buildings on this steep hillside are painted in vivid colors and there is an incredible proliferation of street art (aka graffiti), much of which deserves to be viewed and enjoyed. Old crates that returned empty to Valparaiso, were re-used in the past, so the siding of many homes is made of corrugated iron or other metal. While Valparaiso is a one in a lifetime experience, that unique visit is probably sufficient.
